title: Ferris Bueller's Day Off
logline: A high schooler skips school for a day in Chicago. Fourth-wall-breaking teen comedy.
overview: After high school slacker Ferris Bueller successfully fakes an illness in order to skip school for the day, he goes on a series of adventures throughout Chicago with his girlfriend Sloane and best friend Cameron, all the while trying to outwit his wily school principal and fed-up sister.

jokes.text: Radio traffic report plays while parents frantically call for Ferris — the mundane, cheerful broadcast perfectly counterpoints the domestic panic
jokes.setup: Calm, upbeat radio traffic report about a beautiful Chicago day plays over the scene
jokes.punchline: The serenity of the broadcast is punctured by panicked off-screen cries of 'Ferris? Ferris? Tom!'
jokes.explanation: A classic Hughesian juxtaposition — the sunny, breezy normalcy of the radio against the overwrought parental hysteria. It immediately signals the film's tone: the world is beautiful, the adults are ridiculous. Good structural economy.

jokes.text: 'I'm fine. I can get up... I have a test today... I want to go to a good college, so I can have a fruitful life.'
jokes.setup: Parents are hovering over their 'sick' child, expecting him to need convincing to stay home
jokes.punchline: Ferris proactively protests with increasingly absurd virtue-signaling ('fruitful life'), reverse-psychologying his parents into keeping him home
jokes.explanation: This is sharp character writing. Rather than being caught faking, Ferris has engineered a situation where his parents CONVINCE him to stay home. The escalation from 'I can get up' to 'fruitful life' is a perfect comedic arc in four lines. It's the core of Ferris's character — the manipulative genius disguised as the good kid — delivered with economy and structure.

jokes.text: Jeanie: 'Yeah, right. Dry that one out, you can fertilize the lawn.'
jokes.setup: Dad says Ferris 'doesn't feel well'
jokes.punchline: Jeanie immediately cuts through the act with a sharply worded metaphor equating Ferris's performance with manure
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the reel. It's fresh, it's specific, it has genuine wit — a barnyard metaphor used as a savage sibling put-down. 'Dry that one out' makes it visual and agricultural in a memorably odd way. Jeanie's voice is established instantly: she sees through everything and is furious about all of it. High quotability, genuine originality.

jokes.text: Ferris: 'Jeanie? I can't see that far.' — squinting dramatically at her
jokes.setup: Jeanie has arrived, clearly furious; Ferris has been called out for faking
jokes.punchline: Ferris doubles down on the performance mid-exposure, pretending he can't see his sister who is presumably a few feet away
jokes.explanation: A solid bit of in-the-moment character comedy — Ferris's brazenness in continuing the performance even when exposed is funny. It's not exceptional but it shows his unflappability, which is a key character trait.

jokes.text: Jeanie: 'Bite the big one, Junior.'
jokes.setup: Parents are fawning over Ferris while Jeanie seethes
jokes.punchline: Her only direct communication with Ferris is this blunt, contemptuous dismissal
jokes.explanation: Economy is its strength — three words, completely characterizes the sibling relationship. 'Junior' is the perfect mock-diminutive. It's a little dated but lands as an '80s snap.

jokes.text: Jeanie: 'If I was bleeding out my eyes you guys would make me go to school. This is so unfair.'
jokes.setup: Parents are coddling Ferris while sending Jeanie off to school
jokes.punchline: Jeanie escalates to hyperbolic bleeding-from-eyes imagery to express the disparity, then deflates it with the whine 'This is so unfair'
jokes.explanation: The juxtaposition of grotesque imagery ('bleeding out my eyes') immediately deflated by teenage whining ('this is so unfair') is well-constructed. Jeanie's righteous indignation is entirely earned — she's correct, and that makes it funnier.

jokes.text: Jeanie: 'That's it. I want out of this family.'
jokes.setup: Mom tells Jeanie to 'be thankful' for her health as consolation for Ferris getting to stay home
jokes.punchline: Jeanie's nuclear response to this mild platitude
jokes.explanation: A perfectly timed, disproportionate response. The humor comes from the gap between the mild provocation and Jeanie's complete nuclear option. Solid economy and character work.

jokes.text: Ferris, now alone, breaking the fourth wall: 'It's nice to know that I have such loving, caring parents. You're both very special people.'
jokes.setup: Parents have just delivered saccharine farewell ('Ringy-dingy,' 'pumpkin'), leaving Ferris alone
jokes.punchline: Ferris turns to camera with performative warmth that is simultaneously sincere AND a deadpan observation about their gullibility
jokes.explanation: This is the first confirmed fourth-wall break in the film — a formal introduction of the device and of Ferris as our unreliable, conspiratorial narrator. It works as gentle irony and as a structural announcement.

jokes.text: Dad saying 'Ringy-dingy' as a way to say he'll call
jokes.setup: Dad is giving earnest, caring goodbye instructions
jokes.punchline: 'Ringy-dingy' — a comically dorky dad-ism that punctures the solemnity of his farewell
jokes.explanation: A small but effective bit of character establishment — this is exactly the kind of dorky dad-speak that makes these parents perfectly lovable and credulous. It characterizes them without a lengthy scene.

jokes.text: Tom Bueller: 'Ringy-dingy.' — his sign-off for 'call me'
jokes.setup: Tom is trying to be a warm, accessible dad, telling Ferris to call if he needs anything
jokes.punchline: He punctuates the genuine moment with 'Ringy-dingy' — an oddly dorky, Lily Tomlin-esque phone noise that makes him unexpectedly goofy
jokes.explanation: Specific, slightly absurd word choice that characterizes the dad as a trying-too-hard boomer type. The incongruity of 'ringy-dingy' as a sincere parting word is quietly funny.

jokes.text: Ferris, to camera, with a satisfied smile: 'They bought it.'
jokes.setup: We've just watched Ferris's performance and his parents' complete capitulation
jokes.punchline: Two words. Maximum economy. The audience has been in on the con the whole time — this is Ferris acknowledging us as his co-conspirators
jokes.explanation: One of the great two-word deliveries in '80s cinema. 'They bought it' is perfect in its economy — the relief, the smugness, the conspiratorial delight, all in a satisfied exhale. It earns a high score because the entire opening sequence has been a slow build to exactly this moment, and two words is exactly the right length. It also formally seals the film's relationship between Ferris and the audience. Comparable in economy and structure to the 8.0 anchor.

jokes.text: Ferris, to camera: 'One of the worst performances of my career and they never doubted it for a second.'
jokes.setup: Ferris has just fooled his parents with a theatrical sick act
jokes.punchline: He self-critiques the performance as an artist would — not pride in the deception but mild embarrassment at the quality — implying he's done FAR better and that this was beneath him
jokes.explanation: This is exceptional character writing. Ferris doesn't gloat about fooling his parents — he's mildly chagrined at the low quality of the deception. It reframes his parents not just as credulous but as an unworthy audience. The word 'career' is the key: it implies a long history of performances and a professional standard. This is both funny and definitive character establishment. It's specific to Ferris in a way that no other character in cinema could deliver it. High marks are justified.

jokes.text: Ferris, to camera: 'How could I possibly be expected to handle school on a day like this?'
jokes.setup: Ferris is addressing the audience directly on his philosophy of skipping school
jokes.punchline: The beautiful day is presented as an irrefutable logical argument against school, delivered with complete earnestness
jokes.explanation: A highly relatable line delivered with Ferris's characteristic unassailable confidence. It works because every viewer has had this thought — Ferris simply says it out loud to the camera. Good economy and character voice.

jokes.text: 'This is my ninth sick day this semester. It's getting pretty tough coming up with new illnesses. If I go for 10, I'm probably gonna have to barf up a lung.'
jokes.setup: Ferris has established himself as a skilled faker; he's giving us the inside view of his operation
jokes.punchline: 'Barf up a lung' — the escalation from 'coming up with new illnesses' to this specific grotesque image. The professional problem-solver framing makes the absurdity land harder.
jokes.explanation: The humor is in Ferris treating illness-faking as a craft problem — the ninth day is a creative challenge, not a moral one. 'Barf up a lung' as the logical endpoint of escalating fake symptoms is well-constructed dark absurdism.

jokes.text: Ferris's tutorial: 'The key to faking out the parents is the clammy hands. It's a good non-specific symptom. I'm a big believer in it.'
jokes.setup: Ferris is delivering a how-to guide on faking illness, addressing the audience as a master instructing students
jokes.punchline: 'I'm a big believer in it' — the phrasing of a devoted practitioner talking about a philosophy of life, applied to licking your palms to fake out your parents
jokes.explanation: The comedy derives from the register mismatch: Ferris speaks with the gravity and conviction of a TED talk or medical practitioner about juvenile delinquency tradecraft. 'Non-specific symptom' is clinical medical language. 'I'm a big believer in it' is the language of a methodology advocate. This is high character-integration — only Ferris, the unflappable authority on his own life, delivers this with zero self-consciousness.

jokes.text: 'A lot of people will tell you that a good, phony fever is a dead lock. But you get a nervous mother, you could wind up in a doctor's office. That's worse than school.'
jokes.setup: Ferris is building his case for clammy hands over phony fever in his illness-faking methodology
jokes.punchline: 'That's worse than school' — the punchline flips our expectation; the risk isn't getting caught, it's the unpleasant consequence of too convincing a performance
jokes.explanation: Good misdirection — we expect the risk to be getting caught, but Ferris's risk calculation is entirely different and more absurd: being too convincingly sick. 'That's worse than school' is the perfect deadpan kicker.

jokes.text: 'You fake a stomach cramp and when you're bent over, moaning and wailing, you lick your palms. It's a little childish and stupid, but then, so is high school.'
jokes.setup: Ferris is completing his step-by-step tutorial on clammy-hand generation
jokes.punchline: 'It's a little childish and stupid, but then, so is high school' — after the specific absurd image of palm-licking, the pivot to philosophical dismissal of high school is perfectly timed
jokes.explanation: One of the most quotable lines in the film. The structure is impeccable: (1) bizarre specific image (moaning, wailing, licking palms), (2) apparent self-deprecation ('childish and stupid'), (3) the pivot that reframes the childishness as a feature not a bug ('so is high school'). It's both funny and a genuine philosophical statement. The rhythm of the sentence is excellent. Earns 8+.

jokes.text: 'Life moves pretty fast. If you don't stop and look around once in a while, you could miss it.'
jokes.setup: Ferris has been riffing on his philosophy of skipping school
jokes.punchline: This aphorism lands as simultaneously sincere and comically self-important — a teenager delivering profound life wisdom to justify playing hooky
jokes.explanation: The most famous line in the film and arguably one of the most quoted lines in '80s cinema. It earns its quotability because it's genuinely wise AND funny — the humor comes from a teenager delivering profound unsolicited life philosophy to justify skipping school. The line works on multiple levels: it's Ferris's thesis statement, it's the film's thesis statement, and it's also a bit ridiculous coming from a 17-year-old. Perfect economy. This is a cultural touchstone, which nudges it toward the 9+ range in quotability, though as a craft moment in context it's an 8.

jokes.text: 'I do have a test today. That wasn't bullshit. It's on European socialism. I mean, really, what's the point? I'm not European. I don't plan on being European. So who gives a crap if they're socialists? They could be fascist anarchists. It still wouldn't change the fact that I don't own a car.'
jokes.setup: Ferris pivots to the actual content of the test he's skipping — European socialism
jokes.punchline: The 'argument' escalates from reasonable skepticism to 'fascist anarchists' (a logical oxymoron delivered with confidence) and then completely non-sequiturs to 'I don't own a car' — the real grievance has nothing to do with political science
jokes.explanation: This is one of the best comedy monologues in the reel. The logic is impeccably constructed to seem like an argument while gradually going insane. 'Fascist anarchists' is a deliberate oxymoron that Ferris delivers without irony — it shows he barely knows what these words mean and doesn't care. Then the pivot to 'I don't own a car' is a complete non-sequitur that's the actual emotional core of his complaint. The car becomes a callback setup. This is excellent absurdist character writing.

jokes.text: 'Isms, in my opinion, are not good. A person should not believe in an ism, he should believe in himself. I quote John Lennon: I don't believe in Beatles, I just believe in me. A good point there. After all, he was The Walrus. I could be The Walrus. I'd still have to bum rides off people.'
jokes.setup: Ferris is delivering his philosophy on '-isms', quoting John Lennon as authority
jokes.punchline: The chain of logic goes: isms bad → Lennon quote → 'The Walrus' → 'I could be The Walrus' → still need rides. Each step is a confident non-sequitur, landing on the mundane grievance of needing rides as the endpoint of this philosophical journey
jokes.explanation: The comedy of an increasingly unhinged philosophical chain that keeps landing back on the car problem. 'I could be The Walrus. I'd still have to bum rides' is a beautiful comedic landing — the transcendent (being The Walrus) immediately grounded by the banal (needing rides). Also a callback setup: the car is established as Ferris's real complaint, which pays off when Cameron's Ferrari appears. The structure of the whole rant — Lennon quote as philosophical authority, 'a good point there' as self-approval — is excellent Ferris character writing.

jokes.text: Ferris: 'I could be "The Walrus." I'd still have to bum rides off of people.'
jokes.setup: Ferris has just mused that he could aspire to Lennon-level self-belief
jokes.punchline: The deflation: even if he achieved that philosophical status, the practical problem of having no car remains — returning to the car motif
jokes.explanation: The return to the car problem after the Lennon philosophy detour is structurally satisfying — a callback that also deflates the pomposity of the preceding monologue. 'The Walrus' as an identity aspiration is funny because it's such a strange thing to want to be. Economy is excellent — two sentences do a lot of work.

jokes.text: Economics teacher droning through roll call — 'Bueller? ... Bueller? ... Bueller?' — in a completely flat, nasal monotone with zero variation
jokes.setup: Roll call begins in an obviously tedious classroom
jokes.punchline: The teacher calls 'Bueller?' multiple times with absolutely identical intonation, as if repeating it will produce a different result, embodying total soul-crushing academic tedium
jokes.explanation: One of the most culturally quoted moments in the film. Ben Stein's performance is comedy through pure affect — the absolute flatness of his delivery is itself the joke. The humor is entirely in what ISN'T there: no impatience, no curiosity, no humanity. This is a masterclass in deadpan. The repeated 'Bueller?' with zero emotional variation is funny on first viewing and funnier on rewatch. It earns 8+ for its cultural impact, originality of delivery, and perfect character-integration of 'everything Ferris is running from.'

jokes.text: Student covering for Ferris: 'My best friend's sister's boyfriend's brother's girlfriend heard from this guy who knows this kid who's going with a girl who saw Ferris pass out at Thirty-One Flavors last night. I guess it's pretty serious.'
jokes.setup: Teacher asks about Ferris's absence; a student responds
jokes.punchline: The rumor chain is so elaborately long and remote that it's completely useless as information — and then 'I guess it's pretty serious' delivered with total sincerity as a conclusion
jokes.explanation: One of the great comic constructions of the film. The escalating chain of relational connections is a perfect parody of teen rumor mills — each additional link makes the original source more absurd while the student delivers it with complete confidence. 'Thirty-One Flavors' as the specific dramatic venue is perfect. The deflating button — 'I guess it's pretty serious' — is exactly the right note of casual catastrophizing. 'No problem whatsoever' as the sign-off is an additional perfect beat. This is structurally excellent, well-earned comedy.

jokes.text: Teacher continues calling 'Frye? Frye? Frye?' into apparent dead air — same monotone as 'Bueller' — while Ferris's scene is already underway
jokes.setup: The Bueller roll call gag has just landed; we cut away and return
jokes.punchline: The teacher is STILL doing roll call with the same intonation, suggesting the horror never ends — it's also a visual joke that this classroom exists in perpetual Groundhog Day
jokes.explanation: A callback that extends and deepens the original joke — the teacher's world has not moved on. It's the comedic logic that this classroom is Ferris's alternative: eternal, unchanging, nasal suffering.

jokes.text: Roll call: 'Frye? Frye? Frye?' — with increasingly long pauses and no answer, following the Bueller moment
jokes.setup: We just had the Bueller roll call with one absent student; the teacher moves to the next name
jokes.punchline: Frye is also absent, and the teacher calls the name three times into silence — the joke being that the epidemic of absence is spreading, or that Frye is also with Ferris
jokes.explanation: A quick escalation off the Bueller joke — the idea that multiple students are MIA deepens the comedy of the teacher's futile droning. The repeated 'Frye?' is funny partly because of what precedes it and partly as a visual gag (we can imagine the teacher's flat affect not changing at all). Earns rewatch value because Frye turns out to be Cameron.

jokes.text: Cameron: 'Shredded.' (in response to 'How do you feel?')
jokes.setup: Ferris asks how Cameron feels, expecting to manipulate him into coming out
jokes.punchline: 'Shredded' — a word that implies total destruction, delivered with complete, resigned flatness
jokes.explanation: Economical and character-specific. 'Shredded' is a more vivid and specific word than 'terrible' — Cameron is a person who has examined his own suffering and found the precise adjective. This is good introductory character writing.

jokes.text: Cameron: 'I can't, stupid, I'm sick.' Ferris: 'That's all in your head. Come on over.'
jokes.setup: Ferris just faked being sick for 5 minutes; now he diagnoses Cameron's real illness as psychosomatic
jokes.punchline: The irony of Ferris — who just performed an Oscar-caliber sick performance — dismissing Cameron's actual symptoms as imaginary
jokes.explanation: The irony is built from the preceding scene — Ferris spent five minutes convincingly faking sick, and now he immediately dismisses someone who might actually be sick. The hypocrisy is the joke, and it's completely in character for Ferris.

jokes.text: Ferris: 'I'm sorry to hear that. Now come on over here and pick me up.'
jokes.setup: Cameron has just said 'I feel like complete shit, Ferris. I can't go anywhere.'
jokes.punchline: Ferris's 'sympathy' lasts exactly one beat before he issues the demand anyway — the 'I'm sorry to hear that' is the thinnest possible fig leaf
jokes.explanation: Ferris's character in one line — genuine warmth and total selfishness occupying the same sentence without any cognitive dissonance. 'I'm sorry to hear that. Now come pick me up' is a perfect crystallization of his manipulative charm. It's also structurally impeccable: acknowledgment → dismissal → demand, three beats in one sentence.

jokes.text: Ferris, to camera: 'You're not dying. You just can't think of anything good to do.'
jokes.setup: Cameron has just said 'I'm dying' — Ferris's diagnosis to camera
jokes.punchline: He reframes Cameron's physical suffering as a failure of imagination — the diagnosis is both hilariously dismissive and weirdly accurate
jokes.explanation: One of Ferris's best lines — it's a genuine insight delivered as comedy. Cameron IS dying in a psychosomatic sense, and Ferris's prescription (do something good) is exactly right. The line works as a joke AND as a character revelation. The economy is excellent; it also characterizes Cameron perfectly without describing him.

jokes.text: Ferris, to camera: 'If anybody needs a day off, it's Cameron. He has a lot of things to sort out before he graduates. He can't be wound up this tight and go to college. His roommate will kill him.'
jokes.setup: Ferris is explaining why Cameron needs this day
jokes.punchline: 'His roommate will kill him' — Ferris's concern for Cameron expressed as a practical logistical problem for a hypothetical future roommate
jokes.explanation: Good character writing — Ferris's affection for Cameron is expressed through concern, but the punchline externalizes it as 'his roommate will kill him,' which is both funnier and more Ferris. The logic escalates correctly: wound up → college → roommate murder.

jokes.text: Ferris singing to camera: 'When Cameron was in Egypt's land / Let my Cameron go'
jokes.setup: Ferris is talking about needing to free Cameron from his neurotic self-imprisonment
jokes.punchline: He literally sings a parody of 'Go Down Moses' with Cameron's name substituted, delivered with total commitment
jokes.explanation: Surprising and committed — the sudden lurch into spiritual song about Cameron's liberation is bizarre and funny. It also develops the Cameron-as-enslaved-soul metaphor that underpins the film. Ferris's willingness to do this unironically is very much in character.

jokes.text: 'Pardon my French, but Cameron is so tight that if you stuck a lump of coal up his ass, in two weeks you'd have a diamond.'
jokes.setup: Ferris is characterizing Cameron's anxiety for the audience
jokes.punchline: The coal-to-diamond metaphor applied to Cameron's anal tension — a crude image delivered with Ferris's characteristic precision and 'pardon my French' courtesy
jokes.explanation: One of the great character descriptions in '80s comedy. The joke is a perfect construction: 'Pardon my French' as faux-courtesy before an anatomically crude image; the coal/diamond metaphor as a genuinely clever way to express uptightness; the two-week timeline adding a layer of absurdist specificity. It's graphic but earned — it's a metaphor, not a gross-out gag. This is what distinguishes excellent crude humor from lazy crude humor: it has metaphorical precision. Comparable to or exceeding the 8.0 anchor in craft.

jokes.text: Dean Rooney calls Mrs. Bueller. Mrs. Bueller says: 'Oh my God. I'm so sorry. I just completely forgot to call.' — she's apologizing to the Dean for not reporting Ferris's absence
jokes.setup: Rooney calls to investigate Ferris's absence, expecting to catch the parents covering for him
jokes.punchline: Mrs. Bueller immediately apologizes — not for the deception, but for her own oversight in not calling the school. She's so completely taken in by Ferris's performance that she treats this like a genuine administrative oversight
jokes.explanation: The humor is in Mrs. Bueller's complete sincerity — she is not in on the joke, she is the joke. Her rushing to apologize for the administrative lapse rather than defending Ferris reveals the full depth of her credulity. Good situational irony.

jokes.text: Mrs. Bueller: 'This is all news to me.' Rooney: 'Usually is.'
jokes.setup: Mrs. Bueller expresses shock that Ferris could be skipping school
jokes.punchline: Rooney's 'Usually is' — delivered as a weary aside, the first moment of genuine wit from the antagonist
jokes.explanation: Two words that do enormous work — it characterizes Rooney as someone who has been frustrated by credulous Bueller parents before, and it's genuinely witty. The economy here is as good as it gets. Rooney gets a moment of being actually right, which makes him a better antagonist.

jokes.text: Mrs. Bueller: 'I don't remember him being sick nine times.' Rooney: 'That's probably because he wasn't sick. He was skipping school.'
jokes.setup: Mrs. Bueller is confused about why she doesn't remember nine sick days
jokes.punchline: Rooney explains the logical reason: because they weren't sick days, they were successful cons
jokes.explanation: Functional expository comedy. Rooney spelling out the obvious to the oblivious mother is funny but not inventive. It's solid information delivery with mild comedy rather than a pure joke.

jokes.text: Rooney: 'Wake up and smell the coffee, Mrs. Bueller. It's a fool's paradise. He is just leading you down the primrose path.'
jokes.setup: Rooney is trying to convince Mrs. Bueller that Ferris is manipulating her
jokes.punchline: He stacks three clichés back to back ('wake up and smell the coffee,' 'fool's paradise,' 'primrose path') in rapid succession, undermining his own authority through sheer platitude density
jokes.explanation: The humor is in Rooney's cliché-stacking — a man who considers himself the smartest person in the room cannot construct a sentence that doesn't lean on worn idioms. It characterizes him as pompous but hollow.

jokes.text: Ferris, to camera: 'I asked for a car, I got a computer. How's that for being born under a bad sign?'
jokes.setup: We cut from Rooney's phone call; Ferris is at a computer
jokes.punchline: The juxtaposition of 'born under a bad sign' (heavy blues/tragedy language) with 'I got a computer instead of a car' (a minor, First World inconvenience of a wealthy suburban teen) is perfect
jokes.explanation: The car callback lands here — we now know what Ferris has been complaining about. The comedy is in the register: 'born under a bad sign' is the language of profound suffering applied to an affluent teenager's gadget disappointment. Also reveals that Ferris has computer skills, setting up what comes next.

jokes.text: Cut to: Economics teacher playing a recording of himself droning 'Did you know... Never had one lesson' — implying he's so monotonous he's literally automated his own class
jokes.setup: We've established the teacher's total monotony via the roll call
jokes.punchline: The audiotape playing his voice — 'Never had one lesson' — implies he found playing a recording indistinguishable from his actual presence, confirming he is essentially a machine
jokes.explanation: A clever visual gag — the teacher has literally recorded himself and is playing the tape, suggesting his delivery is so identical to recorded audio that it doesn't matter. It's also a visual joke about the classroom as a space outside of time.

jokes.text: Economics teacher's entire 'Anyone? Anyone? The Great Depression... Anyone? Anyone? Voodoo economics...' sequence
jokes.setup: Teacher asks a series of questions to a room of comatose students
jokes.punchline: The repeated 'Anyone? Anyone?' with zero variation in the face of absolute silence — and then answering his own questions in the same tone — becomes a hypnotic comedy rhythm
jokes.explanation: One of the most culturally impactful comedy sequences of the 1980s. Ben Stein's performance is perfect: the total absence of affect in the face of total student disengagement, culminating in him answering his own questions with 'Voodoo economics' in the same nasal drone. The rhythm of 'Anyone? Anyone?' became a cultural shorthand for academic tedium. It earns high craft scores for structure (the building repetition is carefully constructed), character integration (completely specific to this character), and originality (the joke is in what's absent — energy, life, response). The whole sequence is the highest-scoring single comedic construct in this reel.

jokes.text: Economics teacher: 'Does anyone know what Vice President Bush called this in 1980? Anyone? Something "d-o-o" economics. Voodoo economics.'
jokes.setup: The teacher is continuing his 'Anyone? Anyone?' shtick, now asking about political history
jokes.punchline: He phonetically spells out 'd-o-o' as though he genuinely can't remember the word — then produces 'voodoo economics' — his flat delivery making even a reasonable question feel absurd
jokes.explanation: The 'd-o-o' spelling is particularly funny — it makes the teacher sound like he barely knows his own material, which contradicts his pompous affect. Part of the running 'Anyone? Anyone?' gag, slightly elevated by the specific detail.

jokes.text: Jeanie, responding to condolences about her 'sick' brother: 'What are you sorry for? I have to live with the trouser snake.'
jokes.setup: A classmate says 'I'm really sorry about your brother'
jokes.punchline: 'Trouser snake' — a derisive nickname for Ferris that reframes his charm as predatory and reveals Jeanie's completely different experience of living with him
jokes.explanation: Brilliant Jeanie writing. 'Trouser snake' is simultaneously crude slang and an accurate description of Ferris's charm-based manipulation. It recontextualizes Ferris's charisma from the other side of the glass — he's the snake, Jeanie is not under his spell. The casualness with which she says it ('I have to live with the trouser snake') implies this is simply how she thinks of him. High originality.

jokes.text: Student: 'This guy in my biology class said that if Ferris dies, he's giving his eyes to Stevie Wonder.'
jokes.setup: Classmates are discussing rumors that Ferris is gravely ill
jokes.punchline: Donating eyes to Stevie Wonder — dark absurdism at its best: (a) Stevie Wonder is blind, (b) cornea donors are dead, (c) the student finds this generous enough to report as a touching anecdote
jokes.explanation: One of the best gags in the reel. The specificity of Stevie Wonder (not just 'a blind person' but THE most famous blind person, which makes the student seem even more ludicrous) is perfect. The delivery — 'He's such a sweetie' — treats this morbid donation pledge as an act of generosity rather than dark absurdity. It's a genuinely creative piece of comedy writing.

jokes.text: Student describing his condition to Ferris on the phone: 'Well, did you see Alien? When that creature was in that guy's stomach? It kind of feels like that.'
jokes.setup: Ferris is on the phone asking strangers how he's doing; a student describes his supposed condition
jokes.punchline: The Alien chest-burster as a medical description — a teenager translating physical discomfort into the only frame of reference available to him (a gross-out horror movie)
jokes.explanation: Good pop culture absurdism — the specificity of Alien (1979) as the diagnostic tool is funny and very '80s teenager. The earnestness with which it's delivered sells it.

jokes.text: Student, after the Alien speech: 'Freshmen.'
jokes.setup: The student has been describing Ferris's illness in Alien terms, then pauses
jokes.punchline: 'Freshmen.' — a single-word, contemptuous dismissal, apparently explaining who is responsible for spreading such absurd rumors (or perhaps just said as a general expression of contempt for the grade)
jokes.explanation: One word used as a complete thought. The delivery of 'Freshmen.' as a diagnosis of everything wrong with the situation is funny in its economy and implied hierarchy. Pure teen register.

jokes.text: Student: 'He's getting me out of summer school... I can't handle summer school.'
jokes.setup: Student on phone has been sharing concern about Ferris's health
jokes.punchline: His concern for Ferris is entirely selfish — 'I hope he doesn't die. I can't handle summer school.' — the dark comedy of someone whose grief is purely practical
jokes.explanation: Good dark comedy — the students' concern for Ferris is revealed to be purely self-interested, which is a funny commentary on teenage social capital. Ferris's value to his community is entirely transactional.

jokes.text: Girl on phone: 'Oh my God, you're dying?... Think I may need a kidney transplant... Are you upset?'
jokes.setup: Ferris is managing calls from concerned students; a girl calls to check on him
jokes.punchline: The conversation moves from 'you're dying' to kidney transplants to 'are you upset?' — the clinical emotional management of a teenager who treats her friend's death as a scheduling issue, then pivots to asking if he's available this weekend
jokes.explanation: The girl's progression from dramatic death concern to 'maybe I'll see you this weekend' is funny — it encapsulates teenage emotional shallowness. The 'Think you'll be alive this weekend? Great.' is the best beat here.

jokes.text: Rooney: 'I don't trust this kid any further than I can throw him.' Grace: 'Well, with your bad knee, Ed, you shouldn't throw anybody.'
jokes.setup: Rooney uses the idiom 'I can't trust him as far as I can throw him'
jokes.punchline: Grace takes it literally, noting that with his bad knee he shouldn't be throwing anyone — subverting the idiom by treating it as physical advice
jokes.explanation: Classic idiom-literalization comedy, well-executed. Grace's straight delivery of medical advice in response to Rooney's idiom deflates his pomposity perfectly. The added detail of a 'bad knee' makes it funnier — specific and slightly pathetic. Grace is established here as a deadpan deflator of Rooney's ego.

jokes.text: Grace: 'Well, makes you look like an ass is what he does, Ed.'
jokes.setup: Rooney is delivering a pompous speech about Ferris being a danger to the school's governance
jokes.punchline: Grace cuts directly through the rhetoric: 'makes you look like an ass is what he does, Ed' — the bluntness is the entire joke
jokes.explanation: Grace is one of the film's best comedic assets — she's a secretary who has absolutely zero patience for Rooney's self-importance. The phrasing ('makes you look like an ass is what he does') is specifically constructed to put 'ass' in the most emphatic position in the sentence. The added 'Ed' at the end is perfect deflation. Great economy.

jokes.text: Rooney: 'Thank you, Grace. I think you're wrong.' (unconvincingly)
jokes.setup: Grace has just told him he looks like an ass
jokes.punchline: The formal politeness of 'Thank you, Grace' followed by the clearly unconvincing 'I think you're wrong' — the gap between his composure and his obvious insecurity is the joke
jokes.explanation: Good reaction beat — the deflation is complete when even his rebuttal sounds unconvinced. Jeffrey Jones plays this well and it's funny in context, though it doesn't stand alone.

jokes.text: Grace's taxonomy of the school social hierarchy: 'The sportos and motorheads, geeks, sluts, bloods, wasteoids, dweebies, dickheads — they all adore him. They think he's a righteous dude.'
jokes.setup: Grace is explaining why Ferris is so dangerous to Rooney's authority
jokes.punchline: A middle-aged school secretary rattling off the full '80s teen social taxonomy — including 'slutsf,' 'dickheads,' and 'wasteoids' — with the cadence of a legal brief, concluding with 'righteous dude'
jokes.explanation: The comedy is entirely in character integration: a secretary in her 50s delivering this list with bureaucratic authority. The list itself is a funny '80s artifact, and 'righteous dude' as her conclusion is perfect. It's also a genuine cultural snapshot. High quotability.

jokes.text: Grace: 'Ed. You sounded like Dirty Harry just then.' Rooney, lighting up: 'Really?'
jokes.setup: Rooney has just delivered a pompous speech about catching Ferris; Grace offers a compliment
jokes.punchline: Rooney's instant, transparent vanity at the Dirty Harry comparison — 'Really?' — a man who fancies himself a tough-guy cop in an ill-fitting role
jokes.explanation: Perfect character moment for Rooney. The beat works because his pomposity is immediately reducible to vanity — he doesn't want to be right, he wants to be Dirty Harry. 'Really?' in response to Grace's dry observation is a great reaction beat. His character is summed up: ego over everything.

jokes.text: Cameron on the phone with Ferris: 'I'm serious, man, this is ridiculous. Making me wait around the house for you. Why can't you let me rot in peace?'
jokes.setup: Cameron is resistant to going out; Ferris has apparently been pressuring him
jokes.punchline: 'Why can't you let me rot in peace?' — framing being left alone to suffer as a right, using the language of peaceful death
jokes.explanation: 'Rot in peace' is a great Cameron line — it inverts 'rest in peace' to describe his preferred mode of existence. Highly character-specific to Cameron's particular brand of dramatic self-pity.

jokes.text: Cameron's prolonged phone argument: 'I'm not doing this for me, I'm doing it for you.' Cameron: 'Do you know what my diastolic is?'
jokes.setup: Ferris is pressuring Cameron to come pick him up
jokes.punchline: Cameron responds to Ferris's selfless framing by citing his diastolic blood pressure — the most anxious possible response to a pep talk
jokes.explanation: A perfect Cameron joke — only Cameron would respond to emotional encouragement with a blood pressure reading. It crystallizes his character: hypochondriac, medically anxious, constitutionally unable to respond to anything except catastrophe.

jokes.text: Cameron: 'You've been saying that since the fifth grade.' (in response to 'you can find a new best friend')
jokes.setup: Ferris threatens to find a new best friend if Cameron doesn't come over
jokes.punchline: Cameron calmly notes this is an empty threat with a long history — both they and we know it's meaningless
jokes.explanation: Economic and characterful — Cameron's resigned familiarity with Ferris's manipulation tactics. He knows every move in the playbook and complies anyway. It's both funny and a little sad, which is Cameron's essential register.

jokes.text: Ferris, to his dad, faking weakness: 'All this talking has made me kind of light-headed. I think I ought to lie down.' Dad: 'Take a hot bath and then wrap a hot towel around your head.'
jokes.setup: Ferris is managing a call with his dad while also managing Cameron on hold
jokes.punchline: His dad's completely useless folk remedy advice ('wrap a hot towel around your head') delivered with total confidence and care — the loving but incompetent parent captured perfectly
jokes.explanation: Solid character comedy — the dad's earnest, medically dubious advice ('wrap a hot towel around your head') is funny precisely because it's delivered with total confidence and love. The simultaneous management of dad and Cameron is good structural comedy.

jokes.text: Ferris, to camera: 'I'm so disappointed in Cameron. $20 says he's sitting in his car, debating about whether or not he should go out.'
jokes.setup: Ferris has just hung up and is predicting Cameron's behavior
jokes.punchline: He bets $20 on a very specific prediction about Cameron's exact location and mental state — which we are about to confirm
jokes.explanation: Good payoff setup — Ferris is so confident he knows Cameron that he makes a specific wager with the audience. The specificity ('sitting in his car, debating') is funnier than a general prediction. The rewatch bonus is for knowing Cameron is in exactly that position.

jokes.text: Ferris: 'He'll keep calling me. He'll keep calling me until I come over. He'll make me feel guilty. This... this is ridiculous. Okay, I'll go. I'll go. I'll go.'
jokes.setup: We cut to Cameron, who is sitting in his car exactly as Ferris predicted
jokes.punchline: Cameron's internal monologue perfectly mirrors the manipulation Ferris described — he talks himself into going out using exactly the script Ferris predicted, confirming Ferris knows him completely
jokes.explanation: One of the best structural comedy moments in the reel. The payoff of Ferris's prediction is perfect — Cameron is LITERALLY in his car, LITERALLY debating, LITERALLY talking himself into it. But the real comedic genius is that Cameron's inner monologue is Ferris's script, confirming that Ferris understands him better than Cameron understands himself. 'This... this is ridiculous. Okay I'll go, I'll go, I'll go' is an escalating capitulation delivered as internal monologue that's both funny and subtly moving.

jokes.text: Cameron's escalating outbursts in his car: 'Shit.' (beat) 'Goddamn it!' (beat) 'Forget it. That's it. I'm not going.'
jokes.setup: Cameron has just resolved to go to Ferris; we watch him try to start the car or build resolve
jokes.punchline: Three beats of increasing frustration ending in total reversal — 'I'm not going' — the entire internal resolution collapsed in under 30 seconds
jokes.explanation: Perfect comic escalation and reversal — the three-beat structure is classically constructed (resolve, complication, collapse). The humor is in the speed of the reversal and the gap between his brave decision and his immediate failure. Cameron as a person who cannot follow through on anything, even a decision he just made, is characterization through pure physical comedy and rhythm.

jokes.text: Economics teacher drones on about irony and prison symbolism to a visibly catatonic classroom — a prolonged, deadening silence punctuated only by his monotone voice
jokes.setup: A teacher asks an earnest literary question about prison symbolism and irony to his class
jokes.punchline: The classroom is completely silent and dead-eyed; no one answers or even stirs — the extreme pause IS the joke, taking over ten seconds of silence
jokes.explanation: The long silence from [17:43] to [18:13] is the joke — the irony of a teacher asking about irony while getting no response is a subtle meta-layer. Works on rewatch when you appreciate how Hughes uses the classroom as a counterpoint to Ferris's adventure.

jokes.text: Grace interrupts class to tell Sloane Peterson her grandmother has 'just passed' — an obviously fabricated emergency that is delivered with absurd theatrical concern
jokes.setup: Grace pulls Sloane out of class with exaggerated sympathy: 'My dear, I'm afraid that I'm the bearer of bad tidings'
jokes.punchline: The audience knows this is a total lie cooked up by Ferris; Grace's overwrought performance is completely unearned by the fiction she's delivering
jokes.explanation: The gap between Grace's sincere delivery and the audience's knowledge that the grandmother is alive is the engine. Competent dramatic irony, enhanced on rewatch when you see how straight everyone plays it.

jokes.text: Rooney suspects foul play and gossips with Grace: 'Who's this girl going out with? It's so hard to tell these days. I do see her with Ferris Bueller quite a little bit.'
jokes.setup: Rooney learns a student's grandmother died and immediately pivots to investigating rather than offering sympathy
jokes.punchline: His suspicious instincts are both correct and nakedly petty — he's clearly obsessed with Bueller and can't even process a death without connecting it to his nemesis
jokes.explanation: Rooney's Javert-like fixation on Ferris is perfectly concentrated here. 'It's so hard to tell these days' adds a nicely absurd layer — he's judging Sloane while also surveilling Ferris. High character integration.

jokes.text: Grace asks 'You still want his daytime number?' after 'Mr. Peterson' has already called IN — Rooney's trap has been sprung on him before he could spring it
jokes.setup: Rooney tells Grace to get Mr. Peterson's daytime number so he can call and catch Ferris in the lie
jokes.punchline: Before Rooney can even dial, 'Mr. Peterson' calls him — Grace's deadpan 'You still want his daytime number?' signals the trap has inverted
jokes.explanation: Perfect comic timing compressed into one line. Rooney's plan collapses before it launches, and Grace's deadpan delivery makes it land harder. The economy is exceptional — four words do enormous work reversing the power dynamic.

jokes.text: 'Sure, I'd be happy to. Yeah, you just produce a corpse, and I'll release Sloane. I want to see this dead grandmother, firsthand.'
jokes.setup: Fake grieving father asks Rooney to excuse Sloane so the family can handle funeral arrangements
jokes.punchline: Rooney cuts through the sentiment and demands proof of death — 'just produce a corpse' — a spectacularly callous bureaucratic response delivered with zero self-awareness
jokes.explanation: One of the reel's best lines. 'Just produce a corpse' is darkly funny on its own, but 'I'll dig up your daughter' in the next beat makes it a double-punch. Rooney's willingness to weaponize a grandmother's death against a grieving family is so grotesque it becomes absurdly comedic. Highly quotable, strong character integration — only Rooney, the bureaucratic monster, would say this.

jokes.text: 'Just roll her old bones on over here, and I'll dig up your daughter.'
jokes.setup: Rooney doubles down on demanding proof of a dead grandmother
jokes.punchline: 'Roll her old bones' and 'dig up your daughter' escalate from demanding proof to treating the corpse as a bureaucratic transaction — the phrasing is bracingly tactless
jokes.explanation: This is the reel's standout Rooney line. The phrasing 'roll her old bones on over here' is so casually dismissive of death that it shocks and delights simultaneously. 'I'll dig up your daughter' is a perfect payoff — it inverts the expected sympathy of a school principal and reveals Rooney as a comically malevolent bureaucrat. Approaches the 8.0 anchor threshold comfortably.

jokes.text: Rooney asks 'Was this your mother?' — Fake-Peterson replies 'No, my wife's mother' — Rooney's sympathy evaporates completely at this answer
jokes.setup: Rooney, perhaps softening slightly, checks the relationship between Peterson and the deceased
jokes.punchline: The implied subtext is that Rooney only cares if it's a direct parent; a mother-in-law doesn't warrant the same compassion — his transactional sympathy is exposed
jokes.explanation: A quiet but effective beat. Rooney's question implies a hierarchy of grief, and the 'wife's mother' answer confirms he's about to feel zero obligation. The comedy is in what goes unsaid — classic deadpan economy.

jokes.text: Rooney, thinking he's on a private call, launches into: 'Tell you what, dip-shit, you don't like my policies you can just come on down here, and smooch my big old white butt. Pucker up, buttercup.'
jokes.setup: Rooney thinks he's speaking candidly to 'Peterson' and venting about school policy
jokes.punchline: He calls the grieving father 'dip-shit' and tells him to 'smooch my big old white butt' and 'pucker up, buttercup' — a spectacular failure of professionalism delivered with gleeful aggression
jokes.explanation: 'Pucker up, buttercup' is a great piece of writing — it's the kind of insult that could only come from a specific type of petty authority figure who thinks he's untouchable. The rhyme makes it quotable and slightly absurdist. The escalation from 'dip-shit' to full butt-smooching imagery is perfectly calibrated for maximum shock from a school principal.

jokes.text: Grace interrupts Rooney mid-rant: 'Ferris Bueller's on line two.' — Long beat of horror as Rooney realizes what he just said.
jokes.setup: Rooney has just told 'Peterson' to kiss his butt, believing he's safe to be horrible
jokes.punchline: Grace's flat announcement that Ferris Bueller is on line two immediately recontextualizes everything — Rooney just screamed obscenities at the kid he's been trying to catch
jokes.explanation: Structurally the best joke of the reel. The reveal that 'Peterson' was Ferris all along — announced with Grace's completely flat, oblivious delivery — is a perfect comedic reversal. The pause Rooney takes before 'What?' is implied and devastating. Economy is exceptional: four words from Grace destroy Rooney completely. The joke rewards the audience for paying attention to the setup. Easily comparable to the 8.0 anchor and edges above it.

jokes.text: Ferris calls immediately after the reveal — cheerfully asking about homework assignments, completely unbothered
jokes.setup: Rooney has just realized he screamed obscenities at Ferris while pretending to be someone else; now Ferris calls again
jokes.punchline: Ferris's breezy, polite call about homework — 'I'm not feeling very well today' — is the ultimate troll move; he holds all the cards and uses them to be casually pleasant
jokes.explanation: The juxtaposition of Ferris's sunny homework request against Rooney's just-revealed humiliation is perfectly timed. Character integration is exceptionally high — this is entirely Ferris's brand of effortless domination. 'Have a nice day' as a sign-off after getting everything he wanted is a beautiful button.

jokes.text: Rooney begins profusely apologizing to 'Mr. Peterson' for the obscene rant — 'I really don't know, sir. I mean, I didn't think I was talking to you. I thought I was talking to somebody else.'
jokes.setup: Rooney, caught having screamed 'smooch my big old white butt' at a 'grieving father,' must now grovel
jokes.punchline: His explanation — 'I didn't think I was talking to you, I thought I was talking to somebody else' — is simultaneously true (he was talking to Ferris) and a completely useless defense that makes everything worse
jokes.explanation: The irony of 'I thought I was talking to somebody else' being literally true — he was talking to Ferris — while still being an absurd non-excuse is a clever layer. Rooney's cringe-inducing backpedaling is a great showcase for Jeffrey Jones's performance.

jokes.text: 'Pardon my French, but you're an asshole.' / 'Absolutely right, sir. You've hit the nail right on the head.'
jokes.setup: Ferris, posing as Peterson, loses patience with Rooney's groveling and calls him an asshole directly
jokes.punchline: Rooney's response — 'Absolutely right, sir. You've hit the nail right on the head' — is the ultimate capitulation, agreeing that he is an asshole with the same groveling politeness he was just using
jokes.explanation: Rooney's self-deprecating agreement is a masterclass in character humiliation comedy. 'You've hit the nail right on the head' applied to being called an asshole is brilliantly absurd — he's so desperate not to get sued he's agreeing with everything. The formal register ('Absolutely right, sir') against the content ('you're an asshole') creates maximum tonal contrast. High quotability, strong structure.

jokes.text: 'Bueller, Ferris Bueller.' — Ferris reveals his identity to Rooney at the end of the call
jokes.setup: Rooney has been groveling throughout the call, believing he's talking to an angry father named Peterson
jokes.punchline: Ferris announces 'Bueller, Ferris Bueller' — confirming Rooney's worst suspicion and signing off with his own name as a flex, leaving Rooney in full horror
jokes.explanation: One of the film's most iconic moments. The Bond-style name inversion ('Bueller, Ferris Bueller') is both a pop culture riff and a perfect character moment — Ferris can't resist the showmanship even when he's already won. Economy is near-perfect: three words annihilate Rooney. The reveal doubles as a callback to every 'Bueller? Bueller?' classroom moment. Truly quotable, heavily rewatched.

jokes.text: Cameron, panicking: 'Now, I'm a little scared 'cause what if he recognizes my voice?' Ferris: 'Impossible. You're doing great.'
jokes.setup: The impersonation is over and Cameron is realizing the danger of what he just did
jokes.punchline: Ferris's 'Impossible. You're doing great' is simultaneously reassurance and a dig — Cameron was the one who nearly tanked the whole scheme, and Ferris's breezy confidence is delusional cheerleading
jokes.explanation: A solid character beat — Cameron's anxiety vs. Ferris's pathological optimism. 'Impossible' is funny because Cameron's voice was plenty recognizable; Ferris just doesn't care. Good character integration but not exceptional writing.

jokes.text: Ferris and Cameron argue while Rooney is on hold — Ferris gives Cameron contradictory instructions, Cameron follows them, then Ferris kicks Cameron for following them
jokes.setup: Ferris is whispering directions to Cameron mid-phone-call while Rooney is on hold
jokes.punchline: Ferris tells Cameron to 'cover it, talk, talk, talk' — Cameron says something that blows the scheme — Ferris kicks him — Cameron says 'Why'd you kick me?' — Ferris: 'Where's your brain?' — Cameron: 'I asked you first.'
jokes.explanation: 'I asked you first' in response to 'Where's your brain?' is a great comeback — it's simultaneously a non-answer and a perfect deflection of blame back onto Ferris. The physical escalation (the kick) feeds the comedic chaos cleanly.

jokes.text: "What the hell is wrong with you?" / "Where's your brain?" / "Why'd you kick me?" / "Where's your brain?" / "I asked you first."
jokes.setup: After the phone call ends in partial disaster, Ferris and Cameron immediately start bickering like an old married couple
jokes.punchline: "I asked you first" — a playground-level comeback from two teenagers who just pulled off an elaborate con on a school principal
jokes.explanation: The 'I asked you first' punchline is the right level of juvenile for the characters. The escalating 'where's your brain?' repetition has a nice rhythm. Character integration is solid — this is exactly how these two communicate.

jokes.text: Cameron's grievance list: 'You make me get out of bed. You make me come over here. You make me make a phony phone call to Edward Rooney? The man could squash my nuts into oblivion.'
jokes.setup: Cameron, furious at being kicked, starts listing his complaints about being dragged into Ferris's scheme
jokes.punchline: 'The man could squash my nuts into oblivion' — the escalation from getting out of bed to existential nut-squashing threat is brilliantly disproportionate and very Cameron
jokes.explanation: Cameron's specific, panicked anxiety is on full display. 'Squash my nuts into oblivion' is exactly the kind of hyperbolic worst-case-scenario thinking that defines Cameron — and the phrasing is so specific and colorful it's instantly quotable. High character integration: this speech is completely Cameron.

jokes.text: Cameron dramatically announces 'See you later, pal, I'm going home' and storms off — only to be talked back within seconds by a mild apology
jokes.setup: Cameron threatens to leave, asserting he has agency in this friendship
jokes.punchline: His exit is immediately defused and he returns — reinforcing the running joke that Cameron is entirely incapable of asserting himself against Ferris
jokes.explanation: Cameron's false exits are a character-defining pattern. This one is quickly resolved, so it's more of a grace note than a full joke, but it reinforces his lovable spinelessness.

jokes.text: After apologizing, Ferris adds: 'You did screw up, though, right?' — then immediately starts asking for a 'small favor'
jokes.setup: Ferris has just apologized to Cameron for losing his temper
jokes.punchline: He immediately partially retracts the apology ('You did screw up, though, right?') and pivots to asking for a favor — the apology was entirely instrumental
jokes.explanation: Ferris's sociopathic charm is perfectly captured: the apology lasts approximately 10 seconds before he's extracting something new. 'Not that it was completely your fault' is a beautiful hedge. Pure Ferris.

jokes.text: Ferris introduces the Ferrari 250 GT California — 'Less than 100 were made. My father spent three years restoring this car. It is his love, it is his passion... It is his fault he didn't lock the garage.'
jokes.setup: Cameron narrates the Ferrari in reverent, hushed tones — building up its rarity, the years of restoration, the father's devotion
jokes.punchline: 'It is his fault he didn't lock the garage' — a sudden pivot that reframes the father's vulnerability as culpability, delivered with a flat logic that is both funny and chilling
jokes.explanation: One of the great single-sentence reversals in Hughes's writing. The setup builds reverence — rarity, three years, love, passion — and then 'It is his fault he didn't lock the garage' demolishes it with perfect flat logic. The rhythm is impeccable: three parallel 'It is his...' clauses before the fourth subverts the pattern. This is comparable to the 8.0 anchor and exceeds it in structural elegance. Genuinely quotable and culturally remembered.

jokes.text: 'A man with priorities so far out of whack doesn't deserve such a fine automobile.'
jokes.setup: Cameron is horrified at the idea of taking his father's prized Ferrari
jokes.punchline: Ferris delivers a fake-philosophical verdict on Cameron's dad — framing theft as corrective justice for the father's misplaced priorities
jokes.explanation: Ferris's ability to construct ethical frameworks that justify whatever he wants is a core character comedy engine. 'Priorities so far out of whack' is perfectly pompous and quotable. The sentence sounds profound and is utterly self-serving — that tension is the joke.

jokes.text: Cameron: 'He never drives it. He just rubs it with a diaper.'
jokes.setup: Cameron is trying to defend his father and the car's sacred status
jokes.punchline: His own defense of the car accidentally reveals how pathetic the father's relationship with it is — 'rubs it with a diaper' is both accurate and damning
jokes.explanation: 'He just rubs it with a diaper' is a great line — the specificity of 'diaper' (not cloth, not chamois, a diaper) makes the image both precise and absurd. Cameron inadvertently undermines his own argument while revealing his father's sad priorities. Strong economy and character integration.

jokes.text: Cameron: 'Hey, remember how insane he went when I broke my retainer? Come on, that was a little piece of plastic, this is a Ferrari.'
jokes.setup: Cameron is trying to explain to Ferris why they can't take the car by giving a proportional example
jokes.punchline: The retainer story implies Cameron's father is terrifyingly unhinged about trivial things — the escalation to 'this is a Ferrari' extrapolates a genuinely frightening response
jokes.explanation: The retainer story is a great piece of characterization for Cameron's abusive/cold father. The logic — if a retainer caused insanity, a Ferrari will cause something unimaginable — is sound and funny. Good character integration.

jokes.text: Ferris: 'Mr. Rooney would never believe Mr. Peterson drives that piece of shit.' — Cameron: 'It's not a piece of shit.' — Ferris: 'It is a piece of shit.'
jokes.setup: Ferris argues they can't use Cameron's car to pick up Sloane because it would blow the cover story
jokes.punchline: The completely flat back-and-forth 'It is not a piece of shit' / 'It is a piece of shit' played deadpan is both a great comedic rhythm and a perfect character dynamic
jokes.explanation: A quick, clean comedic exchange. Ferris's flat insistence and Cameron's wounded defense of his unremarkable car is a good character beat. The follow-on — 'I don't even have a piece of shit, I have to envy yours' — is the funnier extension.

jokes.text: 'Don't worry about it, I don't even have a piece of shit, I have to envy yours.'
jokes.setup: Cameron protests that his car is not a piece of shit
jokes.punchline: Ferris pivots to a self-deprecating acknowledgment that he doesn't even own a car — so Cameron's piece of shit is relatively aspirational by comparison
jokes.explanation: Structurally elegant — Ferris defuses Cameron's indignation by instantly one-upping his own insult with self-deprecation. 'I have to envy yours' is a great button. The sentence is funny because it uses 'piece of shit' as an aspirational object, which is an unexpected and original flip.

jokes.text: Ferris's plan to fix the mileage: 'We'll drive home backwards.'
jokes.setup: Cameron points out that Cameron's father knows the mileage and they'll be caught if they put miles on the Ferrari
jokes.punchline: Ferris's completely sincere solution is 'We'll drive home backwards' — a plan with the internal logic of a child that he delivers with total confidence
jokes.explanation: One of the best Ferris lines in the film. 'We'll drive home backwards' is pure Ferris logic — it sounds like it makes sense if you don't think about it, which is exactly his brand. The confidence of the delivery is as funny as the idea itself. Near-perfect economy (four words), and completely character-specific — only Ferris would say this with zero irony. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor and edges above it.

jokes.text: "Whatever miles we put on, we'll take off." / "How?" / "We'll drive home backwards."
jokes.setup: Cameron is worried about the mileage on the odometer being discovered
jokes.punchline: Ferris's completely straight-faced solution — 'We'll drive home backwards' — is absurdist genius: a plan that could only come from a teenager who has never thought about how odometers work
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the reel. The genius of 'We'll drive home backwards' is how completely confident and simple it sounds — Ferris delivers it as an obvious solution, which makes it funnier than any elaborate absurdist premise would be. It's also based on a real misconception (some believe odometers run backwards in reverse), giving it just enough internal logic to land. The setup-punchline ratio is perfect: the question 'How?' sets up maximum expectation of a clever answer. High quotability, high rewatch value. Justifies 8+: it's a genuinely surprising answer delivered with perfect economy and total character specificity — only Ferris would say this with that confidence.

jokes.text: Ferris pitches alternatives to calm Cameron: 'How about we rent a nice Cadillac? My treat. We could call a limo! A nice stretch job with a TV and a bar.'
jokes.setup: Cameron has put his foot down — no Ferrari
jokes.punchline: Ferris immediately escalates through increasingly lavish alternatives — Cadillac, limo, stretch limo with TV and bar — each more absurd than the last, undercut by the fact that he has no money to actually pay for any of this
jokes.explanation: A solid escalation beat that shows Ferris's improvisational desperation. The 'my treat' is funny given that Ferris is a teenager with presumably no money. Not exceptional writing but functional character comedy.

jokes.text: Cut to Rooney's office: Rooney is delivering hollow condolences to Sloane — 'Once again, let me tell you how deeply saddened I am by your loss. I... I had a grandmother, once. Two, actually.'
jokes.setup: Rooney, who moments ago was demanding to see the corpse and calling people dipshits, now has to perform sympathy in person
jokes.punchline: 'I had a grandmother, once. Two, actually.' — His condolence is so thin and awkward that the best he can offer is a tepid claim of grandmother-ownership
jokes.explanation: The gap between Rooney's earlier monstrous callousness and his attempt at warmth here is perfect. 'I had a grandmother, once. Two, actually.' is a great line — the correction ('Two, actually') implies he's reaching for something relatable and coming up completely empty. The 'Two, actually' is the specific word that makes it exceptional.

jokes.text: Rooney quotes funeral liturgy ('Man that is born of woman hath but a short time to live') to Sloane while clearly having no emotional connection to any of it
jokes.setup: Rooney, still performing grief for the fake death, reaches for gravitas with religious scripture
jokes.punchline: The formal liturgy delivered by a man who minutes ago said 'roll her old bones on over here' is an ironic contrast so vast it functions as comedy even in a solemn register
jokes.explanation: The comedy here is contextual rather than textual — it's not funny on its own but lands as dark irony when you remember what Rooney just said. Works better on rewatch when the contrast is fresh in memory.

jokes.text: Sloane sees the Ferrari and says 'I guess that's my dad' to Rooney — Rooney beams and says 'Ed, you're a beautiful man. Thank you for your warmth and compassion.'
jokes.setup: Sloane is being released to meet 'her father' — the Ferrari pulls up with Ferris in disguise
jokes.punchline: Ferris (as the father) compliments Rooney on his 'warmth and compassion' — an absurdist mirror held up to the man who just demanded a corpse as proof
jokes.explanation: Thanking Rooney for 'warmth and compassion' is the perfect callback to his grotesque lack of both. Ferris's ability to simultaneously get what he wants AND mock his enemy to his face is completely on-brand. The irony is thick and the audience is entirely in on it.

jokes.text: Ferris, posing as Sloane's father, greets her with 'Do you have a kiss for Daddy?' — Sloane replies 'Are you kidding?'
jokes.setup: Ferris is playing Sloane's father in front of Rooney — a role that creates obvious awkward subtext since Sloane is his girlfriend
jokes.punchline: Sloane's 'Are you kidding?' lands as both an in-character protest and an out-of-character acknowledgment of how weird this is — and then she presumably does it anyway, right in front of Rooney
jokes.explanation: The incest subtext played for cringe is a sharp Hughes move. 'Are you kidding?' works on two levels — the girlfriend's reluctance to kiss her 'dad' and the meta-awareness that this is a bizarre ask. The cut to Rooney's reaction ('So, that's how it is in their family') makes this a full comedic sequence.

jokes.text: Rooney watches Ferris/Sloane kiss and remarks to no one: 'So, that's how it is in their family.'
jokes.setup: Rooney witnesses what appears to be a father-daughter kiss that is clearly too romantic
jokes.punchline: His flat, resigned comment — 'So, that's how it is in their family' — is Rooney at his most brilliantly oblivious; he doesn't realize it's Ferris, so he genuinely thinks the Petersons are a weird family
jokes.explanation: One of the great single-line reaction jokes in the film. Rooney's complete misread of the situation — he thinks he's judging a dysfunctional family when actually he's watching Ferris get away right in front of him — combined with the deadpan economy of 'So, that's how it is in their family' is superb. The line works without any context and is elevated by its context. High quotability, strong rewatch value.

jokes.text: Ferris's speech to Cameron about the Ferrari: 'The question isn't: What are we going to do? The question is: What aren't we going to do?' followed by Cameron begging 'Don't say we're not going to take the car home. Please don't say we're not going to take the car home.'
jokes.setup: Sloane asks what they're going to do now that she's out of school
jokes.punchline: Ferris's pseudo-profound reframing is immediately decoded by Cameron, who pleads in advance against the inevitable — his dread and Ferris's rhetorical confidence are perfectly contrasted
jokes.explanation: Cameron's desperate double plea — 'Please don't say we're not going to take the car home' — is a great character beat. His anticipatory dread mirrors the audience's recognition that of course they're taking the Ferrari. Good structural payoff on the garage argument.

jokes.text: Cameron: "Don't say we're not going to take the car home. Please don't say we're not going to take the car home."
jokes.setup: Ferris's grand 'What aren't we going to do?' speech launches the day
jokes.punchline: Cameron's interruption — his only concern is the Ferrari — immediately deflates Ferris's grandeur and reveals Cameron's singular obsession with the car's fate
jokes.explanation: The repetition ('Please don't say...') signals Cameron's mounting dread and grounds Ferris's flight of fancy. Good character beat — Cameron can't enjoy a single moment because the car is a ticking bomb in his mind.

jokes.text: "If you had access to a car like this, would you take it back right away? Neither would I."
jokes.setup: Cameron is pleading to take the car home; Ferris is about to gun it
jokes.punchline: Ferris breaks the fourth wall (or addresses Cameron) with a rhetorical question that pre-empts any objection — 'Neither would I' is the punchline, confirming the decision is made and nobody could argue otherwise
jokes.explanation: The direct address to the audience (or Cameron) asking them to agree is a good Ferris move. 'Neither would I' is a satisfying, logical button that also signals the film's ethos. Well-structured and character-appropriate.

jokes.text: Ferris drives the Ferrari at high speed — Cameron screams 'Red line, red line, red line! Ferris, get out!' — a visual/audio comedy sequence of pure terror
jokes.setup: They're in the Ferrari and Ferris is driving
jokes.punchline: Cameron's panicked 'red line' screaming (the tachometer is in the danger zone) and 'Ferris, get out!' captures his absolute terror at the destruction of his father's car
jokes.explanation: Cameron's fear is funny precisely because Ferris is in full joy and Cameron is in full horror. The 'red line' specificity (knowing what the tachometer means in real-time) is a good character detail. Primarily a performance/visual gag — works better on screen than on paper.

jokes.text: Street-level 'Save Ferris' charity collection — a stranger is collecting money claiming Ferris needs a new kidney for $50,000
jokes.setup: We cut to a street scene where someone is collecting donations for 'Save Ferris'
jokes.punchline: The 'Save Ferris' movement has apparently evolved to include a fake kidney charity — Ferris's mythology has taken on completely fictional medical dimensions that people are donating to
jokes.explanation: The escalation of the Ferris mythology to include a fake kidney fundraiser is a great absurdist beat. The specificity of '$50,000' makes it funnier. This is one of the film's running commentary jokes about how Ferris's reputation is entirely independent of reality.

jokes.text: "Go piss up a flagpole." — passerby's response to being asked to donate to 'Save Ferris'
jokes.setup: The charity collector asks a passing woman to donate to save Ferris Bueller's life
jokes.punchline: 'Go piss up a flagpole' — a spectacularly specific, archaic insult delivered with total conviction as a response to a kidney charity pitch
jokes.explanation: 'Piss up a flagpole' is a great insult — specific, old-fashioned, and vaguely surreal. The character integration is lower (we don't know this person) but the line itself is a gem: it's the exact phrase someone would use if they'd been asked one too many times.

jokes.text: Charity collector responds to woman's hostility: 'You heartless wench.'
jokes.setup: The elderly woman has told the collector to 'piss up a flagpole'
jokes.punchline: 'You heartless wench' is a charmingly archaic insult that lands funny because of its formality in the context of a sidewalk charity hustle
jokes.explanation: 'Wench' is a funny word choice — formal, slightly Shakespearean, delivered to an elderly woman who just told you to piss up a flagpole. A good button to the exchange, though it doesn't add much conceptually.

jokes.text: Rooney calls the Peterson home; the answering machine picks up: 'We can't come to the phone right now. We've had a death in the family.'
jokes.setup: Rooney, still suspicious, tries to reach the Petersons to verify the story
jokes.punchline: Even the answering machine is in on the lie — 'We've had a death in the family' is Ferris's scheme reaching into every possible point of contact Rooney might try
jokes.explanation: A satisfying structural joke — Ferris has thought of everything, and even the answering machine mocks Rooney's investigation. The escalation of the scheme's reach is consistent with the film's celebration of Ferris's planning.

jokes.text: Rooney to Grace: 'Grace, Ferris Bueller's behind this. There is no doubt in my mind. And now he's got Sloane Peterson involved in this thing. Her grandmother, too.' — Grace: 'You pinhead.'
jokes.setup: Rooney dramatically announces his certainty about Ferris's guilt
jokes.punchline: Grace's flat 'You pinhead' — responding to Rooney including the dead grandmother as a co-conspirator — is a perfect deadpan deflation of his conspiratorial rant
jokes.explanation: Grace's 'You pinhead' is a great single-word (well, two-word) deflation. The joke is that Rooney is correct in his suspicion but sounds absolutely unhinged when he includes the dead grandmother as a co-conspirator. Grace's dry rebuke is perfectly timed and character-specific — she's the only one who can say this to Rooney.

jokes.text: The Peterson answering machine redirects to the Coughlin Brothers Mortuary — another layer of the elaborate fake-death scheme
jokes.setup: Rooney calls the Petersons; the machine forwards to what sounds like it might be a real number
jokes.punchline: Instead it's the Coughlin Brothers Mortuary — a fake funeral home that has been set up as the final stop in the scheme, complete with a professional-sounding answering message
jokes.explanation: The reveal that the scheme goes all the way to a fake mortuary answering machine is a great escalation. The absurdist detail — 'we'll get back to you as soon as is humanly possible' from a mortuary — has an extra dark layer. This demonstrates Ferris's planning to a comically absurd degree.

jokes.text: Rooney calls the Peterson house and gets a mortuary answering machine: "You have reached the Coughlin Brothers Mortuary. We are deeply sorry we are unable to come to the phone right now..."
jokes.setup: Rooney thinks he's found the Peterson home number and calls to expose the lie
jokes.punchline: The number goes to an actual mortuary — Ferris has redirected calls to a funeral home, completing the death-ruse with black-comedy precision
jokes.explanation: The mortuary redirect is a great gag because it escalates the ruse to an absurd extreme — not only is there a death-acknowledging answering machine, but the follow-up number goes to an actual funeral home. The specificity ('Coughlin Brothers Mortuary') adds to the commitment. Dark and funny.

jokes.text: Rooney's villain monologue: 'I did not achieve this position in life by having some snot-nosed punk leave my cheese out in the wind.' — 'I'm gonna catch this kid and I'm gonna put one hell of a dent in his future.'
jokes.setup: Rooney, fully enraged and embarrassed, commits to catching Ferris
jokes.punchline: 'Leave my cheese out in the wind' is an entirely original, deeply weird expression that sounds like a real idiom but isn't — combined with the pompous 'I did not achieve this position in life by...' framing, it's absurdly over-the-top
jokes.explanation: 'Leave my cheese out in the wind' is a genuinely original piece of absurdist dialogue — it has the ring of a real expression but isn't one, which makes it funnier. Combined with Rooney's grandiose self-importance ('I did not achieve this position in life by...'), the whole speech is a perfect character-comedy set piece. The cheese line alone is quotable and strange enough to stick.

jokes.text: "I did not achieve this position in life by having some snot-nosed punk leave my cheese out in the wind."
jokes.setup: Rooney is delivering a self-motivating speech about catching Ferris
jokes.punchline: 'Leave my cheese out in the wind' is an entirely invented idiom that sounds vaguely wrong — it's not quite a real expression, which makes it funnier; Rooney has the energy of someone who thinks he's being very tough
jokes.explanation: The great thing about this line is that 'leave my cheese out in the wind' is not quite a real idiom — it sounds like it should be but isn't, which makes Rooney's confidence in it funnier. It's specific, weird, and entirely Rooney. High originality because made-up idioms delivered with conviction are genuinely rare and funny. High quotability.

jokes.text: Rooney: 'Fifteen years from now when he looks back on the ruin his life's become, he is going to remember Edward Rooney.'
jokes.setup: Rooney continues his villain speech, projecting Ferris's inevitable doom
jokes.punchline: The grandiosity of Rooney imagining himself as a defining memory in Ferris's ruined future — when the audience knows Ferris is currently having the best day of his life — is rich dramatic irony
jokes.explanation: The dramatic irony is thick — the audience has just seen Ferris effortlessly destroy Rooney in the phone call, and now Rooney imagines himself as the architect of Ferris's downfall. His complete lack of self-awareness makes this funny. 'He is going to remember Edward Rooney' as a threatening statement is unintentionally pathetic and funny for it.

jokes.text: Cameron's list of things that could happen to the parked Ferrari: 'It could get wrecked, stolen, scratched, breathed on wrong, a pigeon could shit on it. Who knows?'
jokes.setup: Ferris wants to leave the Ferrari in a downtown parking garage; Cameron is catastrophizing
jokes.punchline: The list escalates from wrecked/stolen to 'breathed on wrong' and 'a pigeon could shit on it' — the escalation goes DOWN in severity (ending on pigeon shit), which is a funnier structure than escalating up
jokes.explanation: The de-escalating escalation (wrecked → stolen → scratched → breathed on wrong → pigeon shit) is a structurally clever list joke. It goes from serious to trivial, which is funnier than going from trivial to serious because it shows Cameron's inability to prioritize. 'Breathed on wrong' is the gem of the list — it's specific and neurotic in exactly the right Cameron way.

jokes.text: "Do you speak English?" / "What country do you think this is?" — Ferris asks the garage attendant if he speaks English; the attendant responds with indignant sarcasm
jokes.setup: Ferris, worried about communicating his instructions for the Ferrari, asks the attendant if he speaks English
jokes.punchline: The attendant's withering 'What country do you think this is?' punctures Ferris's assumption with maximum efficiency
jokes.explanation: The attendant's comeback is perfect — it's the right amount of contempt for the right amount of presumption. Economy is high: seven words do the full job. The joke is at Ferris's expense, which is a nice reversal.

jokes.text: Ferris: 'You fellows have nothing to worry about. I'm a professional.' Cameron: 'Professional what?'
jokes.setup: Ferris reassures Cameron that the parking attendant is trustworthy
jokes.punchline: Cameron's 'Professional what?' is a perfect deflation — 'professional' implies expertise and legitimacy, neither of which a parking lot attendant demonstrably has
jokes.explanation: Cameron's 'Professional what?' is a great two-word punchline. Its economy is exceptional — it doesn't need to explain why 'professional' is a hollow claim in context; the question does all the work. Very Cameron: he immediately finds the flaw in every argument.

jokes.text: Ferris quips: 'See what a finski can do to a guy's attitude?' — referring to how the $5 tip turned the attendant into a loyal guardian
jokes.setup: The parking attendant has been enthusiastically helpful after getting $5
