jokes.punchline: Ferris's self-satisfied observation about the power of $5 — 'finski' being slang for a five-dollar bill — is ironic since the attendant is about to take the Ferrari for a joyride
jokes.explanation: 'Finski' is a nicely specific period slang that adds texture. The dramatic irony (the audience suspects the attendant will betray this trust) makes the line funnier in retrospect. Good but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Visual gag: The parking attendants immediately take the Ferrari for a joyride the moment Ferris, Sloane, and Cameron leave — cutting to them racing the car through Chicago
jokes.setup: Ferris has just paid $5 and trusted the attendants with the Ferrari; 'Trust me' was the last thing we heard
jokes.punchline: The instant the group is out of sight, the attendants are in the Ferrari and racing it — the payoff is immediate and vindicates Cameron's anxiety completely
jokes.explanation: The joyride sequence is a perfect payoff on two threads simultaneously: Cameron's paranoid catastrophizing and the attendant's breezy 'trust me.' The speed of the betrayal (instant) is what makes it funny. Strong structural payoff and high impact as a visual set piece.

jokes.text: Cut back to the Economics class: teacher looks at Ferris's empty seat and says 'Bless his little heart.' — a wistful non-sequitur about the absent student
jokes.setup: We cut from the Ferrari joyride back to the economics class — Ferris's desk is empty
jokes.punchline: 'Bless his little heart' from the economics teacher — genuinely tender concern for the absent Ferris delivered in the same deadpan drone as his lectures — is an absurd tonal pivot
jokes.explanation: The juxtaposition of the classroom's total lifelessness with the warmth implied by 'Bless his little heart' is quietly funny. The economics teacher, who seemed incapable of human emotion, apparently has a soft spot for the absent Ferris. Good callback to the opening.

jokes.text: "Bless his little heart." — one attendant to another, watching the Ferrari's odometer/after the joy ride
jokes.setup: The attendants have been joy-riding the Ferrari
jokes.punchline: 'Bless his little heart' — a phrase of Southern/folksy affection deployed as the attendant contemplates what they've done to Cameron's car; the gentleness of the phrase against the gravity of the act
jokes.explanation: The affectionate condescension of 'bless his little heart' as a reaction to having just joy-ridden someone's prized Ferrari is a good dark understatement. The folksy warmth of the phrase against the casual destruction is the joke.

jokes.text: 'Nine times.' — Ferris breaks the fourth wall to tell the audience how many times the parking attendants have driven the Ferrari around the block
jokes.setup: We've been watching the attendants joyride; the sequence has been going on a while
jokes.punchline: 'Nine times' — Ferris speaks directly to camera to contextualize the disaster, delivered with flat resignation that implies he has been watching and counting
jokes.explanation: Two words. Perfect. 'Nine times' is the reel's best button — it's delivered to camera (Ferris's fourth-wall meta-commentary), it's the deadpan capper on a full visual set piece, and it's one of the most quoted lines from the film. The economy is as close to perfect as film dialogue gets: two words carry the whole sequence's payoff. The flat delivery implies both that Ferris knew, Ferris watched, and Ferris is not quite as unconcerned as he pretends. Genuinely exceptional.

jokes.text: "Nine times." — final line/title card of the reel, referring to how many times the attendants drove the Ferrari
jokes.setup: We've seen the attendants joy-riding the Ferrari; Cameron's worst fears are being realized
jokes.punchline: "Nine times" — the specificity of the number is the punchline; it's both precise and absurd, and suggests the attendants were methodical about their joy-ride
jokes.explanation: Two words that are among the best in the film. 'Nine times' works because: (1) it's the most economical possible punchline — two syllables doing maximum work; (2) the specificity of nine (not five, not twenty) suggests the attendants were keeping count, which is funnier than a vague 'many'; (3) it's the perfect payoff to Cameron's anxiety arc, the 'professional what?' gag, and Ferris's $5 confidence. The structure is flawless — we've been building to 'how bad is this?' and 'nine times' answers with devastating specificity. High quotability because it's immediately usable as an expression of incredulous quantity.

jokes.text: Cameron, visibly nauseated at the top of the Sears Tower, is told to 'lean forward against the glass' by Ferris
jokes.setup: Cameron has already said he doesn't feel good and wants to leave; they are 1,353 feet in the air
jokes.punchline: Ferris cheerfully instructs the terrified Cameron to press against the glass — the worst possible thing for someone with his anxiety
jokes.explanation: The joke works because it is entirely character-driven: Ferris's oblivious enthusiasm is the perfect foil to Cameron's paralytic fear. The instruction to lean against the glass is a genuinely cruel comic escalation that could only come from Ferris, and Cameron's dread is so well established it hits immediately. High character integration bumps this above average.

jokes.text: "Anything is peaceful from 1,353 feet."
jokes.setup: Ferris says the city looks so peaceful from up here
jokes.punchline: He punctures his own sentiment with a blunt, logical observation — anything would look peaceful from that altitude
jokes.explanation: One of the most quotable lines in the reel. Perfectly economical — six words that undercut the romanticism of the moment with cool, irrefutable logic. It's the kind of wry aside that elevates Ferris from prankster to genuine wit. High economy and quotability; structure is clean setup-then-deflation.

jokes.text: "I think I see my dad."
jokes.setup: The three are pressed against the glass of the Sears Tower, 1,353 feet up, looking down at tiny people
jokes.punchline: Cameron's deeply neurotic fixation on his father is so ingrained that even in this sublime moment, his first instinct is to spot the one person who would ruin everything
jokes.explanation: Four words that land as a genuine laugh and a character revelation simultaneously. The joke only works because we already understand Cameron's neurosis about his father — it is a perfect crystallization of his psychology delivered with impeccable economy. The absurdity of thinking you could identify your father from a thousand feet up is implicit and funny on its own; the fact that Cameron would even look is the real joke. Earns its high score.

jokes.text: "Shit. The son of a bitch is down there somewhere."
jokes.setup: "I think I see my dad" — a moment later
jokes.punchline: Cameron immediately spirals from mild observation into full paranoid panic, reinforcing the depth of his father-terror
jokes.explanation: The two-beat escalation from '#3 I think I see my dad' to this expletive-laden panic is funnier together than either is alone. The escalation is fast and character-perfect; the vulgarity is funny because it's proportionally unhinged for staring down at an ant-sized city.

jokes.text: "You want to get married?" / "Sure." "Today?"
jokes.setup: A romantic moment; Sloane presumably expects a sweet exchange
jokes.punchline: "Today?" — Sloane's breezy, game acceptance is immediately complicated by the casual escalation to 'today,' making the absurdity land
jokes.explanation: The speed of the exchange is the joke — Ferris floats the idea, gets an immediate 'sure,' then the logical follow-up 'today?' punctures the romantic moment with absurdity. It's breezy and fast, perfectly matching Ferris's spontaneous character.

jokes.text: "...you feeling a little awkward about being the only cheerleader with a husband..." "give me one good reason why not."
jokes.setup: Ferris lists all the obvious reasons NOT to get married — too young, no place to live — before landing on the specifically ridiculous detail
jokes.punchline: "Being the only cheerleader with a husband" is the absurdly specific and funny item in the list, then he pivots to 'give me one good reason' as if he's listed no good reasons at all
jokes.explanation: Classic comic list structure: two straight items, then a funny specific, then the pivot. The joke on the specific item (cheerleader with a husband) is vivid and visual. The structure carries it well — 'give me one good reason why not' after listing three reasons is a confident and funny bit of ironic self-contradiction.

jokes.text: "I'll give you two good reasons why not: My mother and my father. They're married and they hate each other."
jokes.setup: Ferris asks for one good reason not to get married
jokes.punchline: Sloane's answer is her parents — who are married and hate each other — delivered as a logical, complete argument
jokes.explanation: Clean setup-and-answer joke with a dark undertone. 'Two good reasons: my mother and my father' is a well-structured bit that gets a beat before the explanation, which is funny and bleak in equal measure. Good economy.

jokes.text: "He loves the car. He hates his wife."
jokes.setup: Sloane uses her parents as proof that marriage is bad; Ferris pivots to his car analogy — 'it's like that car'
jokes.punchline: The analogy's conclusion: her dad treats the car with more love than his wife — stark, bleak, and funny
jokes.explanation: Five words, perfectly structured parallel contrast. The bluntness is the joke. This also foreshadows the film's central tension around Cameron's father and his car — adding thematic resonance that rewards rewatchers, though on first view it lands purely as a dark observational punchline.

jokes.text: "You are Abe Froman?" / "That's right. I'm Abe Froman." / "The sausage king of Chicago?"
jokes.setup: Ferris has used a fake reservation under the name 'Abe Froman'; the maitre d' looks at this teenage kid and doesn't believe him
jokes.punchline: "The sausage king of Chicago" — the specificity of the title is the joke; it is the most ridiculous possible prestigious identity a person could claim
jokes.explanation: One of the most quotable and enduring gags in the film. 'The sausage king of Chicago' is a perfect absurdist title: specific enough to sound real, grandiose enough to be ridiculous, and utterly deflating when applied to a teenager in a sweater vest. The beat the maitre d' gets to pause and repeat the title is perfectly timed. This is the kind of line that gets quoted for decades — it earns its high craft score.

jokes.text: "entre nous, I'm very busy here. Why don't you take the kids and go back to the clubhouse?"
jokes.setup: The maitre d' is trying to dismiss this teenager impersonating a sausage magnate
jokes.punchline: "entre nous" (between us) is a perfect affectation from a snooty maitre d', and "go back to the clubhouse" condescends to them as children in a country club context — the class snobbery is the joke
jokes.explanation: The maitre d' is a well-crafted comic antagonist and his language is perfectly calibrated snobbery. 'entre nous' and 'clubhouse' together paint his condescension vividly. Good character work.

jokes.text: "Snooty?" / "Snotty." / "Snotty?"
jokes.setup: The maitre d' says 'I'm going to have to get snooty'
jokes.punchline: Ferris corrects him — 'Snotty?' — causing both to momentarily lose the thread of their confrontation in a semantic detour
jokes.explanation: A quick, perfectly landed exchange. The comedy is in the meta-breakdown of the confrontation: Ferris, completely unintimidated, derails the whole power dynamic over word choice. The maitre d' auto-correcting himself ('Snotty') and Ferris echoing it back as a question is a great comic rhythm. It also reveals Ferris's unflappable coolness — he controls even this moment.

jokes.text: "Listen, young man, either you take the field trip outside or I'm going to have to call the police." / "The..." / "You're gonna call the police on me?" / "Yes." / "Fine. As a matter of fact, I'll call them myself."
jokes.setup: The maitre d' threatens to call the police as the ultimate authority card
jokes.punchline: Ferris cheerfully volunteers to call the police himself — completely inverting the power dynamic; the threat is useless because Ferris has nothing to fear
jokes.explanation: The joke works on a character level: Ferris is so audacious and confident in his impersonation that the greatest threat the maitre d' can muster — the police — becomes a tool Ferris wields back at him. The 'The...' pause before Ferris jumps in shows he's already five steps ahead. Pure Ferris Bueller character comedy.

jokes.text: "This'll be a hoot."
jokes.setup: Ferris has just offered to call the police himself while Cameron and Sloane look on in horror
jokes.punchline: His breezy, almost cheerful delivery of 'this'll be a hoot' — as if this is a fun afternoon activity — is the whole of his character in four words
jokes.explanation: Four words that are completely Ferris. The archaic, wholesome word 'hoot' deployed in a tense standoff is the joke — it reflects his unshakeable confidence and his genuine delight in chaos. Economy is near-perfect.

jokes.text: "You touch me, I yell 'Rat.'"
jokes.setup: The maitre d' tries to grab the phone back from Ferris during their standoff
jokes.punchline: Ferris's threat is to yell 'Rat' — not 'help' or 'assault,' but 'Rat,' the worst possible thing to shout in a fine dining restaurant, threatening the establishment's reputation rather than making a personal safety appeal
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the reel. The genius is in the specificity: Ferris doesn't threaten to call him a liar or make a scene about him — he threatens the one thing a fine restaurant cannot survive, the word 'Rat.' It's perfectly targeted leverage. The joke is original, economical, and could only come from someone as strategically clever as Ferris. The line has been quoted for nearly four decades.

jokes.text: "I weep for the future."
jokes.setup: The maitre d' watches the chaos of Ferris and his friends at his restaurant
jokes.punchline: His dignified, theatrical lament — 'I weep for the future' — is the perfect snooty villain's reaction to being bested by a teenager
jokes.explanation: The maitre d' is a great comic character and this is his best single line — resigned, pompous, and self-dramatizing. The line is quotable precisely because it's the kind of thing a person with an inflated sense of importance would actually say. It lands as his comic epitaph for this scene.

jokes.text: "A: You can never go too far. B: If I'm gonna get busted, it is not gonna be by a guy like that."
jokes.setup: Cameron begs Ferris to let it go and warns he's going to get busted
jokes.punchline: Ferris's two-point manifesto: infinite audacity is the rule, and the maitre d' is beneath his dignity as an adversary — both are delivered with total calm
jokes.explanation: This is Ferris's thesis statement as a character, and it's funny because it's also genuinely cool. The lettered list ('A... B') gives it the feel of a prepared argument, which is absurd since he's making it up on the spot. 'It is not gonna be by a guy like that' is the kind of principled, slightly arrogant line that makes Ferris mythic rather than merely reckless. High character integration and quotability.

jokes.text: "He's devastatingly handsome."
jokes.setup: Ferris is on the phone with Chez Quis, calling to 'confirm' that the real Abe Froman is in the restaurant — he is asked to describe the person
jokes.punchline: He describes himself ('Leather jacket, white T-shirt, sweater vest') and then adds 'He's devastatingly handsome' — self-complimenting while pretending to be a third party
jokes.explanation: The joke has two layers: the audacious scam itself and Ferris's vanity/self-awareness slipping in. 'Devastatingly handsome' is both funny and very revealing of his character — he can't resist. The delivery in the film (Matthew Broderick's perfectly casual tone) makes this a standout moment.

jokes.text: "It's understanding that makes it possible for people like us to tolerate a person like yourself."
jokes.setup: The maitre d', having been defeated by the phone scam, tells 'Sergeant Peterson' he 'appreciates his understanding'
jokes.punchline: The maitre d' cannot stop being snooty even in defeat — his 'thank you' is laced with condescension toward the police officer
jokes.explanation: The maitre d' cannot help condescending even when he's been completely bested — 'people like us' tolerating 'a person like yourself' is a perfect expression of his snobbery. Good character consistency and a nice button on the restaurant scene.

jokes.text: "Darling, you were wonderful."
jokes.setup: Ferris has just pulled off an elaborate phone scam to secure their lunch reservation
jokes.punchline: Sloane plays the proud partner praising her lead, delivering the line with the affectionate irony of someone who is simultaneously charmed and exasperated
jokes.explanation: A pleasant button on the scene, though it doesn't add much beyond warmth. Sloane is the least comedically developed of the trio; this line is charming but not distinctively hers. Functional.

jokes.text: "Cameron, dear friend, you thought we wouldn't have any fun. Shame on you."
jokes.setup: Cameron was terrified throughout the restaurant confrontation
jokes.punchline: Ferris's mock-scolding 'shame on you' — delivered as though Cameron had committed a moral failing by doubting him — is both funny and revealing of Ferris's self-mythology
jokes.explanation: Good Ferris moment — his paternalistic gloating is part of his charm/obliviousness. The 'shame on you' is lightly funny as a mock moral failing. Mid-tier joke.

jokes.text: Cameron's internal monologue: 'Maybe Ferris isn't such a bad guy. After all, I got a car. He got a computer. But still, why should he get to do whatever he wants, whenever he wants? What makes him so goddamn special? Screw him.'
jokes.setup: Cameron seems to be softening on Ferris after the restaurant triumph
jokes.punchline: The monologue performs a full arc from forgiveness back to resentment in about 20 seconds, landing on 'Screw him' — the speed of the reversal and Cameron's inability to maintain goodwill is the joke
jokes.explanation: Cameron's monologue is a mini character study. The rhythm is classic comic structure: build toward an unexpected resolution, then immediately undercut it. 'Screw him' as the concluding position after a full emotional journey that lasts 15 seconds is both funny and very true to Cameron's tortured psychology. High character integration.

jokes.text: "That's why he's sick all the time. It really bothers him. He's the only guy I know who feels better when he's sick."
jokes.setup: Ferris describes Cameron's twisted home life as the root of his chronic illness
jokes.punchline: "He's the only guy I know who feels better when he's sick" — Cameron's psychological dysfunction has inverted normal human experience; sickness is his comfort zone
jokes.explanation: A genuinely sharp observational line about Cameron that is also touching. The paradox — feeling better when sick — is stated so plainly that it lands as both a laugh and a mini character revelation. It's one of Hughes's best character-insight lines. 'The only guy I know' as a qualifier makes it specific and funny.

jokes.text: "If I had to live in that house, I'd probably pray for disease, too."
jokes.setup: The description of Cameron's house as 'like a museum — very beautiful and very cold, and you're not allowed to touch anything'
jokes.punchline: The logical extreme: if you lived there you'd welcome illness as a valid escape mechanism
jokes.explanation: Extends the Cameron characterization from #22 with a darker, funnier logical conclusion. 'Pray for disease' is vivid and specific. Good economy and bleak humor.

jokes.text: "The place is like a museum. It's very beautiful and very cold and you're not allowed to touch anything."
jokes.setup: Ferris describes Cameron's family home in voiceover
jokes.punchline: The museum metaphor perfectly captures the emotional sterility of the house — beautiful, cold, untouchable — implicitly contrasting with where they just went (an actual museum), adding an ironic layer
jokes.explanation: Nicely economical character description. The triple rhythm — 'very beautiful and very cold and you're not allowed to touch anything' — has a good cadence. The implicit comparison to an actual museum (they're on a museum day trip) gives it a bonus ironic layer. Stronger as writing than as a pure laugh.

jokes.text: "Plus, and I must be honest here, I love driving it. It is so choice. If you have the means, I highly recommend picking one up."
jokes.setup: Ferris has been explaining that taking Cameron's father's Ferrari was for Cameron's benefit — to help him confront his fears
jokes.punchline: He breaks character from his altruistic framing to admit he just really loves the car — the direct-to-camera aside 'if you have the means, I highly recommend picking one up' is a classic Ferris fourth-wall break
jokes.explanation: One of the most quotable Ferris moments in the film. The 'and I must be honest here' self-correction is funny on its own (he's been lying to himself for two sentences), and the pivot to addressing the audience directly with a consumer recommendation is Ferris at his most charmingly shameless. 'If you have the means, I highly recommend picking one up' reads like an ad endorsement and is laugh-out-loud funny. The fourth-wall break is perfectly deployed — a signature Ferris move used at exactly the right moment.

jokes.text: "Well, hello, Jeanie. Who's bothering you now?"
jokes.setup: Jeanie (Ferris's sister) storms into the school office looking for Rooney
jokes.punchline: The secretary's greeting implies this is Jeanie's standard state — always bothered, always complaining — and the familiarity is both funny and lightly devastating
jokes.explanation: A quick, well-observed character beat that tells us everything about Jeanie's standing in the school. The secretary isn't even surprised — this is Jeanie's default mode. Good economy.

jokes.text: "What a little asshole." (Secretary mutters under her breath after Jeanie leaves)
jokes.setup: Jeanie storms out after being snubbed
jokes.punchline: The secretary's perfectly timed, matter-of-fact verdict — 'what a little asshole' — said with the calm of someone confirming a long-held opinion
jokes.explanation: The delivery of this line by a mild-mannered school secretary is a perfect tonal subversion. The bluntness and the casual matter-of-factness are the whole joke. The audience has been waiting for someone to say this about Jeanie, and the fact that it's the quiet secretary (not a peer) makes it land harder. Excellent economy and reaction beat — it rewards the audience for their own feelings about Jeanie.

jokes.text: "Four thousand restaurants in the downtown area. I pick the one my father goes to."
jokes.setup: They are at the restaurant and Cameron has spotted his father
jokes.punchline: The odds are astronomical — and Cameron's luck is characteristically catastrophic; this is perfect Cameron-universe logic
jokes.explanation: Cameron's cosmic bad luck is perfectly distilled here. The specificity of '4,000 restaurants' is funny because it quantifies the impossibility of his situation. Pure Cameron character comedy.

jokes.text: "Only the meek get pinched. The bold survive."
jokes.setup: Cameron says they're 'pinched for sure' upon seeing his father at the restaurant
jokes.punchline: Ferris delivers a mock-philosophical maxim with complete confidence — 'the bold survive' as a universal law — and immediately acts on it
jokes.explanation: One of Ferris's best aphorisms. The structure — contrasting meek and bold in parallel clauses — gives it the feel of a proverb, which is funny because it's being applied to sneaking past your friend's dad in a restaurant. The line is memorable and highly quotable, and it perfectly encapsulates his philosophy.

jokes.text: "Les jeux sont faits. Translation: The game is up. Your ass is mine."
jokes.setup: Rooney has tracked down the Bueller house and believes he has Ferris trapped
jokes.punchline: Rooney's theatrical French proclamation followed by 'your ass is mine' is the perfect absurd combo — pompous academese and crude triumphalism in consecutive sentences
jokes.explanation: Rooney quoting French at an empty porch is inherently funny, and the pivot from translated French to 'your ass is mine' is a great tonal contrast. The pretension deflated by vulgarity is classic comedy. Good character work for Rooney — this is exactly what he would say.

jokes.text: "What's the score?" / "Nothing, nothing." / "Who's winning?" / "The Bears."
jokes.setup: Ferris and Cameron are at a Cubs baseball game; someone asks who's winning during a 0-0 game
jokes.punchline: "The Bears" — the wrong sport entirely, delivered with deadpan certainty by someone clearly not paying attention
jokes.explanation: One of the most elegant jokes in the film. The structure is perfect: 'nothing, nothing' sets up a mundane answer, 'who's winning?' is a reasonable follow-up, and 'The Bears' — a football team at a baseball game — is a small, perfectly timed absurdist non-sequitur. It's funny, it's Chicago-specific, and it's utterly economical. The delivery of the wrong-sport answer with apparent confidence is key.

jokes.text: "Think I broke my thumb." — said casually after a foul ball ricochets off his thumb
jokes.setup: Cameron is trying to heckle at the ballgame and something hits his thumb
jokes.punchline: His completely flat, matter-of-fact 'think I broke my thumb' — not crying or complaining dramatically, just announcing it like a weather update — is pure Cameron
jokes.explanation: Cameron's stoic relationship with physical suffering is a character note. The understatement ('think I broke') is funnier than 'I broke' — the casual uncertainty about his own injury is very Cameron.

jokes.text: "Do you realize if we played by the rules, right now we'd be in gym?"
jokes.setup: They are sitting in the bleachers at a Cubs game, in the sun
jokes.punchline: The alternative — gym class — contextualizes the entire day's adventure as a rational risk/reward calculation; the joke is that he's right
jokes.explanation: The joke works on multiple levels: it's a perfect justification for the entire film's premise, it's funny because gym class is the worst possible counterpoint to their day, and it's a rare moment of Ferris making a purely logical argument rather than an aspirational one. Highly quotable and perennially relatable.

jokes.text: Ferris's automated sick-voice recording: "I'm afraid that in my weakened condition I could take a nasty spill down the stairs and subject myself to further school absences. You can reach my parents at their places of business. Thank you for stopping by. I appreciate your concern for my well-being. Have a nice day."
jokes.setup: Rooney rings the Bueller doorbell expecting to confront Ferris
jokes.punchline: Instead of Ferris, an elaborate pre-recorded sick voice plays — the message is not just an excuse but a fully pre-planned, legally-hedging, politely-dismissive automated system deployed to handle exactly this scenario
jokes.explanation: One of the best comedic constructions in the film. The gag has multiple layers: (1) Ferris has a pre-recorded message for exactly this scenario, implying vast preparation; (2) the message anticipates every legal objection — 'subject myself to further school absences' — with malpractice-lawyer precision; (3) it's sweetly polite, which makes it funnier; (4) Rooney is completely impotent against it. The specificity of 'further school absences' as a liability concern is a genuinely original comic idea. This earns a high craft score.

jokes.text: Rooney rings again; the EXACT SAME RECORDING plays a second time
jokes.setup: Rooney has just heard the recording once and shouted at the door
jokes.punchline: He rings again and gets the identical recording verbatim — the repetition and Rooney's growing impotent rage are the escalation
jokes.explanation: The second playing of the recording is funnier than the first. The audience now knows exactly what's coming, and the joke is that Rooney walked right into it again. The machine's indifference to his authority is the ultimate humiliation for a dean of students. Perfect escalation and structure.

jokes.text: "Damn it." — Rooney steps in mud in the garden
jokes.setup: Rooney, determined to get inside the Bueller house after being denied at the front door, goes around the back
jokes.punchline: He immediately steps in mud — a small, undignified humiliation that kicks off a slapstick sequence in his increasingly pathetic attempt to break in
jokes.explanation: The mud is the first beat of Rooney's slapstick degradation sequence. Standard physical comedy but well-deployed — the audience is rooting for the house to defeat him, and it obliges immediately. Not particularly original but functional escalation.

jokes.text: "Damn it." — Rooney, after the second recording, then "Oh, mud." as he steps in something in the garden
jokes.setup: Having been twice outwitted by a recording, Rooney is now navigating the Bueller property alone and frustrated
jokes.punchline: His foot goes into mud — the universe compounding his humiliation with physical degradation
jokes.explanation: Classic authority-figure-being-degraded comedy. Stepping in mud is a standard humiliation beat, but it works here because it's one more layer in an escalating sequence of Rooney's dignity being stripped away. The prim 'Oh, mud' is a funny Victorian-sounding reaction to stepping in dog waste territory.

jokes.text: "Bueller, you son of a bitch." — Rooney muttered into the garden
jokes.setup: Rooney is skulking around the back of the house, increasingly disheveled and desperate
jokes.punchline: His quiet, filthy, bitter curse muttered into the void — no one hears it, it accomplishes nothing — is the perfect expression of his impotence
jokes.explanation: Four words that land perfectly. The specificity of using the student's last name in a curse ('Bueller, you son of a bitch') is a specifically teacher-villain mode of hatred. The futility of the moment is the joke.

jokes.text: "My shoe." — Rooney loses his shoe in the mud
jokes.setup: Rooney has been blundering through the garden
jokes.punchline: His shoe is sucked off by the mud — delivered with pained resignation rather than outrage
jokes.explanation: Standard slapstick escalation — after mud, he loses the shoe. Functional but not inventive. The understated 'my shoe' delivery is funnier than any outburst would be.

jokes.text: "My shoe." — Rooney, apparently losing a shoe in the mud/garden mishap
jokes.setup: Rooney is already muddied and frustrated; now he loses a shoe
jokes.punchline: The bare minimum reaction — just 'My shoe' — from a grown man losing footwear in someone's backyard while trying to bust a teenager
jokes.explanation: Good physical comedy escalation. The two-word delivery ('My shoe') has the right understated panic. It's the right length — longer would be over-explaining, shorter is impossible. Part of the extended Rooney humiliation sequence that builds well.

jokes.text: "Not sure about this family." — Rooney, inside the house
jokes.setup: Rooney has broken into the Bueller house and is creeping around
jokes.punchline: His mild, almost clinical verdict — 'not sure about this family' — after committing illegal trespass is a magnificent piece of understated self-unawareness
jokes.explanation: Five words that are genuinely funny. Rooney has broken into a student's home and is judging THEM. The perfect irony of the trespasser finding the homeowners 'suspicious' — deployed with total deadpan economy — makes this one of Rooney's best lines in the reel.

jokes.text: "Hi, doggie." — followed by "Stay, boy. No, no. Stay. Stay. Sit. Heel. Stay."
jokes.setup: Rooney, inside the house, encounters the Bueller family dog
jokes.punchline: The sequence of increasingly desperate commands to the dog — 'sit, heel, stay' — with decreasing confidence implies the dog is not cooperating; what follows (implied attack) is the escalating slapstick payoff
jokes.explanation: Classic slapstick setup with the authority figure reduced to begging a dog for compliance. The escalating commands ('stay... no no... stay... sit... heel... stay') build comic tension through repetition and imply growing desperation. The visual payoff (implied) is funny even reading just the transcript.

jokes.text: "It's getting late, buddy, we better go get the car back home." — Cameron's panic vs. Ferris's casual response about having 'until 6:00'
jokes.setup: They are at the Von Steuben Day Parade and Cameron is spiraling about the car and time
jokes.punchline: Ferris's completely calm 'we have until 6:00' against Cameron's panic — Ferris doesn't experience time the way Cameron does
jokes.explanation: A reliable Ferris/Cameron dynamic beat. The contrast is well-established by now; this is a functional comic exchange rather than an outstanding one.

jokes.text: "Nothing good." — Cameron's answer to 'what have you seen today?'
jokes.setup: Ferris, exasperated, asks Cameron what he has seen today — clearly hoping Cameron will recognize the magnificence of their day
jokes.punchline: Cameron's flat 'nothing good' after a day that included the Art Institute, a Cubs game, the Sears Tower, and a five-star restaurant lunch is perfect in its stubborn ingratitude
jokes.explanation: Two words that perfectly capture Cameron's psychological state. After everything they've done, 'nothing good' is simultaneously funny, sad, and entirely consistent with his character. Ferris's incredulous reaction makes the joke land harder. High character integration.

jokes.text: "We went to a museum, we saw priceless works of art. We ate pancreas."
jokes.setup: Ferris lists the highlights of their day to convince Cameron it was worthwhile
jokes.punchline: "We ate pancreas" — the list of dignified cultural activities is suddenly punctured by the reminder that sweetbreads are literally an organ, delivered with the same gravitas as the museum
jokes.explanation: Classic comic list structure — two elevated items, then the unexpected third. 'We ate pancreas' is funny purely for the blunt anatomical accuracy; nobody calls sweetbreads a pancreas in polite company, and Ferris saying it with the same register as 'priceless works of art' is the whole joke. Great economy and structure.

jokes.text: "He's licking the glass and making obscene gestures with his hands."
jokes.setup: Ferris has disappeared; Cameron and Sloane look for him and spot him somewhere in the crowd
jokes.punchline: His location is revealed through Sloane's deadpan report — Ferris, wherever he is, is licking glass and making obscene gestures, behavior that is completely unexpected but entirely consistent with his character
jokes.explanation: The joke works on the gap between expectation and report. 'What's he doing?' sets up a mundane answer; instead we get licking glass and obscene gestures. The calm specificity of Sloane's delivery ('and making obscene gestures with his hands' — as opposed to what, with his feet?) is itself funny. Great visual gag described in dialogue.

jokes.text: "He'd just do it just to make me sweat." — Cameron about whether Ferris went back to school
jokes.setup: Cameron is spiraling about where Ferris went; Sloane suggests maybe he went back to school
jokes.punchline: Cameron's 'he'd do it just to make me sweat' — the idea that Ferris is capable of such a specific act of psychological manipulation — is both a funny paranoid Cameron thought and also probably true about Ferris
jokes.explanation: Good Cameron characterization — his paranoia about Ferris has a foundation in reality, which makes this funny and a little sad. Mid-tier joke.

jokes.text: "Ferris! Get off of the float! What are you doing? Get off the float! I can't believe you. How'd you get up there? You're out of your mind!"
jokes.setup: Ferris has appeared on a parade float performing to the city of Chicago
jokes.punchline: Cameron and Sloane's overlapping, panicked, incredulous reaction — the logical human response to this situation — is itself the punchline to the whole sequence
jokes.explanation: The reaction beat matters here — 'how'd you get up there?' is a genuinely funny specific question in the stream of outrage, because it focuses on the logistics rather than the insanity. The overlapping incredulity is a good button on the float gag.

jokes.text: Cameron and Sloane discussing futures: 'What are you interested in?' / 'Nothing.' / 'Me neither.'
jokes.setup: Ferris is established as the guy who can do anything; Cameron and Sloane are musing seriously about their futures and what they're interested in
jokes.punchline: Both admit to being interested in absolutely nothing — delivered with complete earnestness and mutual recognition
jokes.explanation: The two-word punchline ('Me neither') lands because it's perfectly economical and deeply character-true. These are aimless teenagers, and their shared nihilism is funny precisely because it's mutual and unashamed. Strong character integration — this couldn't come from Ferris.

jokes.text: 'What do you think Ferris is gonna do?' / 'He's gonna be a fry cook at Venus.'
jokes.setup: The earnest question about Ferris's future, following the reverence with which both speak about him being able to do anything
jokes.punchline: The deflating, absurdly specific non-answer — 'fry cook at Venus' — subverts the godlike buildup with a mundane destiny
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'Venus' elevates this above a generic deflating joke. It's also quietly affectionate — Cameron isn't really putting Ferris down, he's acknowledging that someone that charming doesn't need a career plan. Good economy and structure.

jokes.text: Ed Rooney baby-talking his dog: 'Poochie, poochie, poochie. Look what Uncle Ed has for you, you little fucker.'
jokes.setup: Rooney has been established as a stern, authoritarian principal obsessed with catching Ferris. We cut to him at home, apparently in a tender moment with his dog.
jokes.punchline: The baby-talk baby voice transitions seamlessly into 'you little fucker' — the violent deflation of the cozy register is the joke
jokes.explanation: This is exceptional character comedy. The register shift — from saccharine pet-talk to casual profanity, with zero tonal acknowledgment — perfectly encapsulates Rooney's barely-suppressed aggression. It's entirely specific to him. The line is immediately quotable and reveals character while getting a big laugh. Comfortably earns an 8.

jokes.text: Jeanie discovering proof that Ferris faked being home — her exclamation 'I knew it!'
jokes.setup: Jeanie has been furiously trying to expose Ferris throughout the film; she sneaks into the house looking for evidence
jokes.punchline: Her triumphant 'I knew it!' confirms what the audience already knows — the comedy is her vindicated outrage
jokes.explanation: Functional plot beat with mild comedic charge. The audience already knows the truth, so the comedy is entirely in Jeanie's smug vindication. Competent but not particularly inventive.

jokes.text: Ferris's voice on the answering machine: 'Ferris. Bueller.'
jokes.setup: Rooney calls the Bueller house expecting to catch someone; the answering machine picks up
jokes.punchline: The machine simply announces 'Ferris. Bueller.' — the name drop as an institution, echoing Rooney's own iconic roll-call cadence against him
jokes.explanation: Sharp callback that inverts the power dynamic: Rooney's own monotone cadence is now weaponized against him by Ferris's answering machine. The economy is perfect — just two words. Strong character integration and structural elegance.

jokes.text: Cameron's incredulous rant: 'You're psychotic. You are, man. You're out of your goddamn mind. I can't believe you went on a goddamn parade float!'
jokes.setup: Ferris has apparently just performed on a parade float in downtown Chicago — an act of absurd public recklessness
jokes.punchline: Cameron's escalating catalog of disbelief ('psychotic... out of your goddamn mind... went on a goddamn parade float!') lands as pure reactive comedy
jokes.explanation: Cameron as straight man is well-deployed here. The triple escalation of increasingly specific outrage is structurally sound. The comedy is mostly in delivery and character truth — Cameron's apoplectic anxiety contrasting with Ferris's breezy confidence.

jokes.text: Ferris doing an impression of himself at the microphone: 'Yeah, yeah. This tune is one of my personal favorites.'
jokes.setup: Cameron is in disbelief about the parade; Ferris is completely unbothered and fondly recreates the moment
jokes.punchline: His self-satisfied impression — delivered as if he's narrating a beloved memory — is the joke; his shamelessness IS the character
jokes.explanation: Ferris quoting himself with evident delight is a perfect character moment. It's self-referential without being meta in a winking way — it's just utterly true to who he is. High character integration score is warranted.

jokes.text: 'Who'd believe that I was in a parade? Who the hell am I? Besides, anybody who would nail me wouldn't go to a parade.' / 'My mother would.' / 'I'm not worried about your mother.'
jokes.setup: Ferris argues he won't be caught because no one who could get him in trouble would attend a street parade
jokes.punchline: Cameron's instant 'My mother would' introduces a specific threat; Ferris's dismissive 'I'm not worried about your mother' caps it — implying he could charm her too
jokes.explanation: Tight three-beat exchange. The punchline is funny because 'I'm not worried about your mother' could mean both 'she won't attend' and 'I could handle her anyway' — the ambiguity is slyly charming. Good economy and clean structure.

jokes.text: "My mother would." / "I'm not worried about your mother."
jokes.setup: Ferris argues that only uptight people who'd want to catch him wouldn't attend a parade.
jokes.punchline: Cameron's straight-man interjection — 'My mother would' (go to a parade AND rat him out) — is immediately deflated by Ferris's breezy dismissal of Cameron's mother as a threat.
jokes.explanation: A four-word exchange that's nearly perfect in construction. Cameron's 'My mother would' is the ideal straight-man callback to Ferris's smugness, and Ferris's instant 'I'm not worried about your mother' is both dismissive and oddly sincere. It's character comedy at peak economy — two lines tell us everything about both of these people and their friendship dynamic. Among the best-constructed micro-exchanges in the reel.

jokes.text: Jeanie's phone call to 911: 'It's real nice that you hope my brother's feeling better, but I'm in danger, okay? I am very cute. I am very alone. And I'm very protective of my body. I do not want it violated, or killed, all right? I need help! Speak-a de English? Dickhead.'
jokes.setup: Jeanie is genuinely scared — there is an intruder in the house. She calls 911 for help.
jokes.punchline: Her plea escalates from logical ('I'm in danger') to hilariously self-absorbed ('I am very cute') to desperate and finally to outraged name-calling at the dispatcher
jokes.explanation: The escalation from genuine distress to 'I am very cute' is a beautiful tonal break — it reveals Jeanie's vanity at the worst possible moment. The sequence builds well and 'Speak-a de English? Dickhead.' is a genuinely funny closing beat. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Jeanie announces to the house: 'I'd also like to add that I have my father's gun and a scorching case of herpes.'
jokes.setup: Jeanie has warned the intruder that the police are coming and that her father has a gun — a sensible deterrent
jokes.punchline: She adds 'a scorching case of herpes' as a secondary deterrent — the non-sequitur is so absurd and self-incriminating it becomes the biggest laugh of her sequence
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the film. The joke is structurally flawless: the first deterrent (gun) is rational, so we expect another rational threat. 'Scorching case of herpes' is a perfect misdirection — it's both utterly absurd and oddly logical as a deterrent while being completely self-sabotaging. The word 'scorching' is inspired. It's highly quotable, earns its shock, and reveals character (Jeanie's desperation and her willingness to say anything). Comfortably an 8+ by the anchor standards.

jokes.text: 'He got my keys!' — Rooney, as the valet drives off in his car
jokes.setup: Rooney has been stalking the garage where the kids picked up Ferrari; now a valet mistake leaves him stranded
jokes.punchline: The world's most put-upon principal has his car stolen by a valet on top of everything else
jokes.explanation: Functional slapstick escalation in Rooney's humiliation arc. Not particularly inventive but serves the running gag of his terrible day. The 'You shithead!' follow-up adds a little character color.

jokes.text: 'You shithead!' — Rooney yelling after the departing valet
jokes.setup: Rooney's car has just been driven away by an oblivious valet
jokes.punchline: His eruption of profanity — a man of authority reduced to screaming impotently at a retreating car — is pure character comedy
jokes.explanation: Minor beat but consistent with Rooney's character disintegration. The principal whose authority has completely collapsed — shouting profanity on a public street — is an enjoyable image even if the joke itself is thin.

jokes.text: Cameron reveals the odometer reading with unsettling precision: 'One hundred and twenty-six and halfway between three and four-tenths.'
jokes.setup: Ferris asks how many miles the car had when they left, clearly setting up a problem
jokes.punchline: Cameron's disturbingly exact answer — including the decimal fraction — reveals he has been monitoring the odometer obsessively; the precision itself is the joke
jokes.explanation: Exceptional character integration. That Cameron tracked the odometer to the nearest tenth — and remembered it perfectly — tells us everything about his anxiety disorder in a single throwaway line. The specificity IS the joke: a normal person would say 'around 126.' Cameron is not normal. This earns its high character score.

jokes.text: 'Here's where Cameron goes berserk.' — Ferris, as Cameron realizes the mileage problem, delivered as a calm narrator
jokes.setup: Cameron is on the verge of a breakdown upon seeing the odometer; this would normally be played as pure dramatic tension
jokes.punchline: Ferris breaks the fourth wall to narrate his best friend's imminent breakdown with total detachment — 'Here's where Cameron goes berserk' — as if he's a documentary filmmaker
jokes.explanation: One of the film's best fourth-wall breaks. The deadpan narration of a friend's psychological crisis — delivered with complete calm — is both funny and slightly chilling. It tells us Ferris has watched Cameron break down before. The economy ('goes berserk' as the entire verdict) is perfect. The meta-narration device is used sparingly enough that it still lands with impact.

jokes.text: Cameron pretends to be catatonic/too sick to come to the door, then immediately recovers when he thinks it might be a nurse: 'Oh, I'm sorry. I can't come to the door right now... God bless the police. I'm saved.'
jokes.setup: Cameron has been in a catatonic state; someone knocks. He launches into an elaborate weak-and-dying act.
jokes.punchline: The instant the possibility of a nurse arrives, Cameron's mortal weakness vanishes and he springs up with gleeful energy — instantly revealing the performance was strategic
jokes.explanation: Good character comedy — Cameron's hypochondria and teenage boy priorities coexist hilariously. The misdirection (he's really sick vs. he's performing) has a satisfying reversal. Slightly undercut by the length of the bit.

jokes.text: The 'nurse' begins reciting: 'Headache, fever, and a chill. I came to help restore your pluck / 'cause I'm the nurse who likes to...' — and then the implied bawdy rhyme cuts off
jokes.setup: The doorbell rang and Ferris implied it might be a nurse; Cameron sprang to life. A woman in a nurse costume begins a flirtatious rhyme.
jokes.punchline: The rhyme cuts to Cameron's reaction before she finishes, leaving the obviously dirty punchline to the audience's imagination — which is funnier than saying it
jokes.explanation: The cut-before-the-punchline technique is well-executed here. Letting the audience complete the joke themselves is good comedy craft. The setup rhyme is slightly hacky (fever/pluck rhyme scheme) but the structural choice to cut is sound.

jokes.text: Ferris's aside about Cameron: 'I think Cameron might have blown a microchip or two. He's always been a little keyed up.'
jokes.setup: Cameron has just had a full breakdown/catatonic episode over the odometer situation
jokes.punchline: 'Always been a little keyed up' is the most spectacular understatement for clinical anxiety disorder ever rendered
jokes.explanation: Ferris's breezy understatement of Cameron's obvious psychological crisis is consistent character comedy. 'Microchip' as a metaphor for Cameron's overwrought brain is a nice touch. The affection underneath the dismissal is what makes it land rather than feel cruel.

jokes.text: Ferris on Cameron's romantic future: 'If things don't change for him, he's gonna marry the first girl he lays. And she's gonna treat him like shit... She won't respect him. 'Cause you can't respect somebody who kisses your ass. Just doesn't work.'
jokes.setup: Ferris is musing to camera about Cameron's emotional immaturity and inexperience with love
jokes.punchline: The armchair psychology escalates to the bluntly cynical 'you can't respect somebody who kisses your ass. Just doesn't work.' — delivered as universal wisdom
jokes.explanation: Ferris as amateur philosopher is a core comedic mode of the film. The observation is genuine and dark, the bluntness is funny, and 'just doesn't work' as a mic-drop closer is economical. Slightly undercut by the length of the monologue that precedes the punchline.

jokes.text: 'Cameron, I could flip out real easy, too. It's okay. Sooner or later everybody goes to the zoo.'
jokes.setup: Ferris is trying to coax Cameron out of his catatonic state with sympathetic reassurance
jokes.punchline: 'Sooner or later everybody goes to the zoo' as wisdom-dispensing comfort is an absurdist non-sequitur — the zoo is a bizarre metaphor for breakdown, delivered as profound truth
jokes.explanation: Genuinely odd and funny line. 'Goes to the zoo' as idiom for losing one's mind is an invention Hughes commits to completely, and Ferris delivers it like it's self-evident truth. The absurdist confidence is what sells it. High quotability — it's the kind of line people repeat.

jokes.text: Cameron 'wakes up' from apparent unconsciousness: 'Ferris Bueller, you're my hero.'
jokes.setup: Ferris and Sloane have been genuinely panicking that Cameron might be really sick or dead; the tension is real
jokes.punchline: Cameron opens his eyes and delivers a cheerful 'Ferris Bueller, you're my hero' — revealing the catatonia was at least partially a performance, and undercutting all the concern
jokes.explanation: Perfect misdirection payoff: the dread evaporates instantly with six words delivered at peak sincerity. The line is quotable, the timing is structurally immaculate, and Ferris's genuinely surprised 'You're kidding?' adds a grace note. This earns its high scores.

jokes.text: Cameron's reaction: 'You bitch. Oh, you son of a bitch.' — Ferris realizing Cameron had been faking
jokes.setup: Cameron says 'you're my hero,' revealing he was more conscious than he let on
jokes.punchline: Ferris's delighted/indignant 'You bitch. Oh, you son of a bitch.' is the perfect response — equal parts impressed and betrayed
jokes.explanation: Good reactive beat. The double 'bitch / son of a bitch' escalation reads as affectionate ribbing between close friends rather than genuine anger, which is the right register. Competent character comedy.

jokes.text: 'Come on. Tarzan.' / 'Sheena!' — Ferris and Cameron's exchange as they rough-house/play
jokes.setup: The tension of Cameron's fake-out catatonia has just broken; they're friends again
jokes.punchline: The wordplay of Tarzan/Sheena — Ferris calling Cameron 'Tarzan' (he just swung back to life), Cameron retorting with Sheena (his jungle queen counterpart) — is playful absurdism
jokes.explanation: Light physical comedy beat. The Tarzan/Sheena riff is a small playful moment that re-establishes the boys' friendship after the tension. Not a major joke but functional tonal reset.

jokes.text: Police officer to Jeanie: 'Drugs?' / Jeanie: 'Thank you, no. I'm straight.' / Officer: 'I meant, are you in here for drugs?'
jokes.setup: Jeanie has been picked up by police and is sitting in a waiting room; an officer addresses her
jokes.punchline: She interprets 'Drugs?' as an offer rather than an inquiry — the misunderstanding reveals both her presumption and the officer's flat affect
jokes.explanation: Classic misdirection setup. The single-word question 'Drugs?' is brilliantly ambiguous, and Jeanie's earnest 'Thank you, no. I'm straight' is the perfect wrong interpretation. The deadpan clarification lands cleanly. Good economy throughout.

jokes.text: Jeanie's fellow detainee's exchange: 'Why are you here?' / 'Drugs.' / 'I don't know why I'm here.' / 'Why don't you go home?' / 'Why don't you put your thumb up your butt?'
jokes.setup: Jeanie is now talking to a burnout guy in the waiting room — clearly a stoner with no illusions about why he's there
jokes.punchline: 'Why don't you put your thumb up your butt?' is both a perfect non-sequitur comeback and a window into this character's chaotic energy
jokes.explanation: The stranger's reply is a great little bit of character writing — his 'Drugs' admission is bluntly honest, and the thumb comeback is a good piece of juvenile surrealism. Establishes a fun dynamic for the scene.

jokes.text: 'You wear too much eye make-up.' / 'My sister wears too much. People think she's a whore.'
jokes.setup: The waiting room stranger critiques Jeanie's appearance out of nowhere
jokes.punchline: Jeanie doesn't defend herself — she redirects to her sister, and the clinical 'people think she's a whore' is delivered with zero affect as if this is simply a fact of life
jokes.explanation: The pivot from self-defense to casual family defamation, delivered with total equanimity, is a good piece of character comedy. The bluntness of 'people think she's a whore' in this context lands because she says it with the tone of 'people think she's a good student.'

jokes.text: 'Blow yourself.' — Jeanie, when the boy asks if she wants to talk about her problem
jokes.setup: The boy in the waiting room, having just been rude, now attempts a kind of therapy session with Jeanie
jokes.punchline: Jeanie's two-word dismissal is perfectly calibrated — contemptuous, dismissive, and funny precisely because it's so disproportionate to a mild question
jokes.explanation: Economy score is high because two words do maximum work. The joke is in the total disproportionality of the response. Character-consistent for an angry, humiliated Jeanie.

jokes.text: 'I know what's wrong. I just wanna hear you say it.' / 'In a nutshell, I hate my brother.' / 'How's that?' / 'That's cool.' / 'Did you blow him away or something?' / 'No, not yet.'
jokes.setup: The boy pushes Jeanie to articulate her problem; she admits she hates her brother
jokes.punchline: 'Did you blow him away or something?' — an escalation to murder — is met with 'No, not yet.' The 'not yet' implies genuine future intent, which is darkly funny
jokes.explanation: 'Not yet' is a good dark punchline. The exchange also has a nice rhythm: the boy's casual assumption that sibling hatred = murder is funny and characterizes him well. 'In a nutshell, I hate my brother' is also a solid piece of deadpan.

jokes.text: 'Then your problem is you.' / 'Excuse me?' / 'Excuse you.' — the boy turning Jeanie's deflection back on her
jokes.setup: The boy has just diagnosed that Jeanie is really just angry that Ferris doesn't get caught
jokes.punchline: Jeanie's reflexive 'Excuse me?' — a social challenge — gets returned as 'Excuse you.' — which agrees with her indignation while redirecting it at her
jokes.explanation: Economical and sharp. 'Excuse me?' / 'Excuse you.' is a perfect one-word twist that recontextualizes her phrase while also being philosophically correct. Good wordplay with actual meaning behind it.

jokes.text: 'There's somebody you should talk to.' — the boy, clearly about to say Ferris — / 'If you say Ferris Bueller, you lose a testicle.'
jokes.setup: The boy has been playing amateur therapist and is about to recommend someone for Jeanie to talk to — the audience and Jeanie both know who he means
jokes.punchline: Jeanie's pre-emptive threat — 'you lose a testicle' — is an escalating comic threat that acknowledges and subverts the obvious setup simultaneously
jokes.explanation: Genuinely excellent. The joke operates on two levels: it's funny as a threat (the specificity of 'a testicle' rather than 'your life' is inspired), and it's structurally clever as a meta-punchline that arrives before the punchline it's preempting. Jeanie's explosive protectiveness about her feelings regarding Ferris is perfect character work. High quotability, deserves its score.

jokes.text: 'Oh, you know him?' — the boy, completely unfazed after the testicle threat
jokes.setup: Jeanie has just threatened castration if the boy says Ferris Bueller's name
jokes.punchline: His completely unrattled 'Oh, you know him?' — as if the threat never happened — is the best possible response; deadpan indifference to a castration threat
jokes.explanation: Perfect deadpan capper to the testicle threat. Four words, complete indifference to a physical threat, and the implication that Ferris Bueller is famous even among the police station's drug detainees. The economy score is nearly perfect — this couldn't be tighter.

jokes.text: Cameron asks Ferris if he watched Sloane change by the Jacuzzi while Cameron was supposedly catatonic — Ferris's confused 'Did you?' and Cameron's 'You saw me? I thought you were catatonic.'
jokes.setup: In what appears to be a touching moment of recovery and friendship, Cameron asks Ferris something unexpectedly intimate
jokes.punchline: The reveal that Cameron — supposedly catatonic — was watching Sloane (Ferris's girlfriend) change, and the mutual awkwardness of 'you saw me? I thought you were catatonic' is perfect cringe comedy
jokes.explanation: A wonderfully uncomfortable beat. Cameron's catatonic episode now retroactively has a creepy asterisk. Ferris's 'Did you? / You're kidding?' reaction, followed by Cameron's sunny 'That's okay. I'm not embarrassed.' is a perfect character reveal — Cameron isn't embarrassed because he was out of it; he's not embarrassed because he genuinely isn't. The character integration is strong.

jokes.text: "Did you see me change out of my clothes by the Jacuzzi? Did you? You saw me? I thought you were catatonic."
jokes.setup: Cameron has just had a sincere emotional breakthrough and the mood is tender and hopeful.
jokes.punchline: Sloane breaks the mood by suddenly asking if Cameron watched her change — revealing she was paying attention to something very different during his supposed catatonia.
jokes.explanation: A great tonal pivot — Hughes is very good at puncturing sincere moments with awkward comedy. Sloane's revelation that she changed near the pool while Cameron was 'catatonic' opens a whole new angle on what he was actually doing. 'I thought you were catatonic' is the perfect straight-man response. The rewatch value is high because Cameron's earlier catatonia gains a new reading.

jokes.text: "That's okay. I'm not embarrassed." — Cameron's response to being caught watching Sloane change
jokes.setup: Sloane has just caught Cameron watching her change while pretending to be catatonic.
jokes.punchline: Instead of embarrassment or denial, Cameron offers a breezy 'I'm not embarrassed' — which only makes it more uncomfortable for everyone, particularly Sloane.
jokes.explanation: A beat that works because it subverts the expected cringe response. We expect Cameron to be mortified; instead his casualness is funnier and more character-consistent — this is the new, slightly more self-possessed Cameron post-breakdown.

jokes.text: 'I better check on the car.' — Cameron's abrupt subject change after the Jacuzzi revelation
jokes.setup: The Jacuzzi revelation hangs in the air; Cameron just announced he's not embarrassed about watching Sloane change
jokes.punchline: The clumsy pivot to 'I better check on the car' deflects from the weirdness in the most transparently avoidant way possible
jokes.explanation: Functional transition joke. The awkward pivot back to the car problem acknowledges the weird moment without dwelling on it. Mild laugh, primarily a tonal reset.

jokes.text: 'The miles aren't coming off.' / 'The miles aren't coming off going in reverse.'
jokes.setup: The plan to run the car in reverse to roll back the odometer has been tried; Cameron reports the result
jokes.punchline: The double delivery — first the bad news, then the clarification that the method (reverse) doesn't work — lands as a slow-build deflation joke
jokes.explanation: The two-beat delivery (problem → failed solution) is competent. The comedy is partly in the mundane specificity — of course the reverse trick doesn't work — and partly in Cameron having actually tried it.

jokes.text: Ferris: 'Well, I thought that might be a problem. Just have to crack open the odometer, roll it back by hand.'
jokes.setup: The reverse trick failed; the mileage problem seems unsolvable
jokes.punchline: Ferris casually produces the next plan — crack open the odometer — as if this is obvious, with no acknowledgment of how ridiculous this escalation is
jokes.explanation: Ferris's breezy solution-escalation is consistent character comedy. The humor is in his confidence about an increasingly absurd plan. Functional but not exceptional.

jokes.text: 'No. Forget it. Forget it.' — Cameron's calm refusal, triggering the film's emotional turn
jokes.setup: Ferris proposes yet another cover-up plan; Cameron has been anxiously going along with everything all day
jokes.punchline: The utter calm of 'Forget it' after a day of mounting panic is the comedic surprise — the hysteria is gone, replaced by eerie serenity
jokes.explanation: This sits at the boundary of comedy and drama, but the comedic element is real: the punchline is the total absence of Cameron's anxiety, which has been his defining trait. The deflation of his panic into 'Forget it' is a form of deadpan that also serves major character development. High character integration.

jokes.text: 'I'm bullshit.' — Cameron, as part of his self-revelation monologue
jokes.setup: Cameron is working himself up to a moment of personal clarity and resolve
jokes.punchline: Using 'I'm bullshit' as a self-description — not 'full of bullshit' or 'bullshitting myself,' but simply 'I am bullshit' — is an oddly funny grammatical construction
jokes.explanation: Minor laugh at the construction 'I'm bullshit' — the ungrammatical self-indictment has an awkward poetry. The scene is trending more dramatic than comedic here, but the phrasing itself is funny enough to count.

jokes.text: Cameron's full breakdown on the Ferrari: 'I'm so sick of his shit! I can't stand him, and I hate this goddamn car! / Who do you love? Who do you love? You love a car. You son of a bitch.'
jokes.setup: Cameron's emotional resolution speech has been building; he decides to confront his father by destroying the prized Ferrari
jokes.punchline: His address directly to the car — 'Who do you love? You love a car. You son of a bitch.' — is a moment of absurdist cathartic comedy; he's having a full argument with an inanimate object on behalf of himself-as-child
jokes.explanation: The climax of Cameron's arc is simultaneously genuinely moving and funny in a cathartic way. 'You love a car. You son of a bitch.' addressed to the Ferrari is perfect — it externalizes his father's indifference by making the car the actual villain. The character integration is as high as it gets; this is entirely and uniquely Cameron's joke/moment. The comedy and drama are inseparable here.

jokes.text: Cameron stares at the dented Ferrari and says 'I dented the shit out of it' — a massive understatement for what is clearly catastrophic damage
jokes.setup: The Ferrari — Cameron's father's prized, obsessively protected car — has just been destroyed by rolling backwards out of the garage and crashing through the glass wall
jokes.punchline: Cameron's matter-of-fact assessment 'I dented the shit out of it' wildly undersells the total destruction visible to the audience
jokes.explanation: The understatement is perfectly calibrated to Cameron's character — his entire arc has been paralyzing anxiety about this exact car. The gap between 'dented' and 'obliterated through glass' is the joke, and it's deeply character-integrated.

jokes.text: Jeanie observes the total destruction of the Ferrari and simply says 'Good.'
jokes.setup: The Ferrari has just been destroyed; everyone is in shock
jokes.punchline: Jeanie's one-word verdict 'Good.' — delivered with complete satisfaction — is both funny and reveals her entire attitude toward Ferris's schemes finally having consequences
jokes.explanation: One word doing the work of a paragraph. The economy is flawless — 10/10. Jeanie's entire subplot crystallized into a single syllable. It's a genuinely exceptional moment of comedic economy and character integration. The audience has been waiting for this release valve. Earns its 8+ score because nothing could be funnier or more efficient here.

jokes.text: Cameron, newly emboldened after a breakdown, announces: 'I can't wait to see the look on the bastard's face.'
jokes.setup: Cameron has spent the whole film terrified of his cold, car-obsessed father; a breakdown over destroying the Ferrari has paradoxically freed him
jokes.punchline: He now relishes the confrontation he was dreading seconds ago — the reversal is both funny and emotionally resonant
jokes.explanation: The humor comes from the total character reversal — the most anxious person in the film is now practically gleeful about the confrontation he feared most. It's funny because it's earned by everything that preceded it.

jokes.text: Cameron asks 'What'd I do?' twice in disbelief; Ferris flatly responds: 'You killed the car.'
jokes.setup: Cameron's nervous rhetorical question 'What'd I do?' is clearly denial — the Ferrari is in a ravine
jokes.punchline: Ferris's completely calm, clinical diagnosis 'You killed the car' treats a Ferrari-destroying catastrophe like a minor household incident
jokes.explanation: Classic straight-man deadpan delivery on a catastrophic event. 'You killed the car' is a perfectly economical punchline — three words that reframe a tragedy as a clinical observation. High quotability, excellent structure.

jokes.text: Ferris volunteers to take the blame, saying 'He hates me anyway' as though that settles the matter
jokes.setup: Ferris is offering to take the heat for destroying Cameron's father's prized Ferrari
jokes.punchline: His casual aside 'He hates me anyway' is offered as a reasonable logical justification — as if hatred is simply a resource to be optimized
jokes.explanation: Ferris's breezy logic — 'he already hates me so it costs me nothing' — is funny because of its oddly pragmatic framing of personal hatred as a fungible asset. Distinctly Ferris's voice.

jokes.text: Cameron and Ferris rapid-fire argue over who gets to take the blame for destroying the Ferrari — 'No, I'll take it.' 'No, I'll take it.' — escalating into Cameron insisting he WANTS the punishment
jokes.setup: Normally people argue over who gets out of trouble; these two are arguing over who gets to be in trouble
jokes.punchline: The reversal — competing for blame rather than innocence — escalates to Cameron delivering the remarkable line 'It is possible to stop Mr. Ferris Bueller, you know?' with quiet pride
jokes.explanation: The whole film's dynamic gets inverted in this exchange. Cameron's small moment of self-assertion — 'It is possible to stop Mr. Ferris Bueller' — is funny precisely because it's the first time he's claimed any agency, and he's using it to embrace punishment. The structure of two people arguing to take blame is an elegant inversion of a classic comedy setup.

jokes.text: Cameron insists on taking the blame in an escalating back-and-forth, culminating in: 'It is possible to stop Mr. Ferris Bueller, you know?'
jokes.setup: Ferris and Cameron argue over who gets to take the blame — a noble contest that keeps escalating
jokes.punchline: Cameron delivers the meta-joke acknowledgment that Ferris is stoppable, delivered with sudden self-awareness and comic authority
jokes.explanation: Cameron's line 'It is possible to stop Mr. Ferris Bueller, you know?' is a small gem: it's the passive, anxious Cameron asserting agency for the first time, but phrasing it with the formal third-person 'Mr. Ferris Bueller' makes it both pompous and endearing. The escalating argument structure builds to this nicely, and it earns its laugh because Cameron's growth is emotionally genuine.

jokes.text: Ferris's mom on the phone with the police station, unaware her son has been out all day, says 'I hope your son is feeling better' — the cop responds 'Tell him all the guys at the station are pulling for him'
jokes.setup: Ferris has been faking illness all day; his mother sincerely believes he's sick at home
jokes.punchline: The police officer has presumably heard about 'Save Ferris' and earnestly passes along well-wishes — the irony is that half of Chicago is cheering for a healthy truant
jokes.explanation: A satisfying callback that layers dramatic irony — the audience knows everything Ferris's mom doesn't. The cop's genuine concern for a perfectly healthy con artist is a lovely payoff to the 'Save Ferris' gag.

jokes.text: Ferris's mom pauses after the cop's well-wishes, processes the absurdity, and says simply: 'Oh, right.'
jokes.setup: She has just been told 'all the guys at the station are pulling for Ferris'
jokes.punchline: Her 'Oh, right' suggests she is performing comprehension she doesn't have — going along with it rather than questioning it, which is the perfect dumb-mom beat
jokes.explanation: A functional reaction beat. The oblivious parent is a well-worn comedy archetype but it's executed cleanly here.

jokes.text: The cop at the desk watches the Bueller mother-daughter chaos and dryly notes to his partner: 'She's a little hyper.' Partner: 'Yeah.'
jokes.setup: Jeanie has been frantically demanding to leave the police station in an increasingly unhinged way
jokes.punchline: The cops' completely flat, unbothered assessment 'She's a little hyper / Yeah' treats the chaos with bureaucratic indifference
jokes.explanation: A reliable deadpan cop beat. The understatement works but the characters are generic — could be any two cops in any movie.

jokes.text: Jeanie's parting shot to the guy she met at the police station: 'Let's not ruin this with a lot of talk, all right?'
jokes.setup: Jeanie is about to be dragged away by her mom; she and the guy she met in holding have had a moment
jokes.punchline: Her breezy, slightly absurd sign-off — treating a rushed police-station flirtation like a mature adult relationship moment — is funny for its incongruity
jokes.explanation: A nicely economical line that reframes an awkward teen moment as though Jeanie is a jaded adult. The incongruity between her age/situation and the sophisticated dismissiveness is the joke.

jokes.text: Guy asks for Jeanie's name. She says: 'It's Jean, but a lot of guys call me Shauna.'
jokes.setup: A simple request for a name
jokes.punchline: The completely unexplained alias 'Shauna' — with the casual implication that she maintains two identities for different social contexts — is a strange, funny non-sequitur
jokes.explanation: The 'Shauna' detail is a small absurdist gem. It raises more questions than it answers and is funnier for being completely unexplained. A unique character detail that lands as an offhand laugh.

jokes.text: After Ferris shouts 'I love you!' and Sloane shouts back 'I love you, too!', Sloane turns to herself and says dreamily: 'He's gonna marry me.'
jokes.setup: A romantic goodbye between Ferris and Sloane
jokes.punchline: Sloane's calm, satisfied internal monologue — delivered directly — is funny for its confident certainty, reducing the romance to a transaction she has already closed
jokes.explanation: Four words, perfectly placed after a romantic moment, that reframe the entire relationship dynamic. Sloane's completely composed, transactional certainty is both funny and character-revealing.

jokes.text: Ferris's mom, lecturing Jeanie about the police station embarrassment, reveals: 'I was gonna take my commission and buy Ferris a car.'
jokes.setup: Mom is scolding Jeanie for costing her the Vermont deal and embarrassing the family
jokes.punchline: The punchline that she was going to spend the money on Ferris — the person who caused all of this — perfectly encapsulates Jeanie's core complaint about the family dynamic
jokes.explanation: This line is a perfect payoff to Jeanie's arc. The cruel irony — that the punishment for Jeanie's day comes with the revelation that the reward was going to Ferris anyway — is both hilarious and genuinely mean-spirited in the best way. It fully validates Jeanie's grievances comedically. Earns the 8 because the structure is impeccable and the character integration is total.

jokes.text: Dad sees papers scattered everywhere and laments: 'God, look at this mess. Paper all over the place. I'll never get this back in order.'
jokes.setup: Dad has just had an apparently chaotic day; he arrives home to find papers everywhere
jokes.punchline: His concern is entirely about paper organization while his wife is furious and his daughter is in trouble — his obliviousness to the family drama is the joke
jokes.explanation: A mild observational joke about the dad's oblivious priorities. It's functional but not particularly sharp — the oblivious-dad-focused-on-the-wrong-thing is a well-worn archetype.

jokes.text: Jeanie: 'I can't drive when you're yelling at me!' — screamed back at her yelling mother, while driving erratically
jokes.setup: Mom is screaming at Jeanie to slow down and stop driving badly
jokes.punchline: Jeanie screams back that the yelling is what's causing the bad driving — a classic self-defeating logic loop, delivered at top volume
jokes.explanation: A recognizable family-argument comedic beat. The circular logic works but is a well-worn comedic device. Competent execution.

jokes.text: Ferris, while racing home in a desperate sprint through neighborhood yards and streets, somehow has the presence of mind to greet a stranger mid-run: 'Hi, how you doing? Ferris Bueller.'
jokes.setup: Ferris is in a full panic sprint trying to get home before his parents
jokes.punchline: He casually introduces himself by full name to a random stranger mid-sprint — his social instincts so ingrained they override survival mode
jokes.explanation: This is a gem of character comedy. The joke requires no setup beyond who Ferris is — his charm and social ease are so foundational that even in a life-or-death sprint, he can't help networking. 'Ferris Bueller' as a self-introduction during a panicked run is perfectly economical and deeply character-specific. Earns the 8+ because no other character in film could deliver this line and have it land the same way.

jokes.text: Dad catalogues Jeanie's offenses — speeding ticket, another speeding ticket, losing the Vermont deal — then says: 'I think we should shoot her.'
jokes.setup: Dad is listing the day's disasters caused by Jeanie in a tone of mounting exasperation
jokes.punchline: His clinical conclusion 'I think we should shoot her' delivered in the same exhausted-dad register as the rest of the list — the casual escalation from 'speeding ticket' to 'execution' is the joke
jokes.explanation: Classic dark escalation joke — the list builds to an absurd extreme delivered as though it's a perfectly reasonable conclusion. The 'shoot her' lands because Dad's affect never changes. Good economy and structure.

jokes.text: Jeanie enters the house to find Principal Rooney in her kitchen, holding the shoe she lost fleeing him earlier, saying: 'Looking for this?'
jokes.setup: Jeanie spent part of the day fleeing Rooney; she lost a shoe in the process — both she and Rooney ended up at the Bueller house separately
jokes.punchline: Rooney's smug 'Looking for this?' with the shoe is a gotcha moment that's also deeply absurd — the principal is in the kitchen holding a shoe like a Bond villain
jokes.explanation: The setup-payoff across the film pays off beautifully here. The visual of Rooney holding a single shoe with that triumphant line is a compact, well-constructed callback that also serves as misdirection — we expect Rooney to be catching Ferris, not Jeanie.

jokes.text: Rooney announces he's 'got' Ferris; then delivers a full villain monologue about having him 'right where I want you' — only for Ferris's parents to burst in calling 'Ferris, we're home!'
jokes.setup: Rooney has finally located what he believes is evidence that Ferris was out all day — he delivers a triumphant villain speech to himself
jokes.punchline: The parents' cheerful 'Ferris, we're home!' immediately deflates the monologue — Rooney's big moment is obliterated by the banal arrival of Ferris's oblivious parents
jokes.explanation: Classic comic deflation — a villain's big moment undercut by perfect timing. The structure is tight: Rooney escalates to maximum menace, then the most domestic possible interruption collapses it instantly.

jokes.text: Rooney, now trapped, turns from predator to pursuer-of-favor, asking Ferris: 'So, how would you feel about another year of high school? Under my close personal supervision.'
jokes.setup: Rooney had Ferris cornered, then lost the advantage the moment the parents arrived; now he's trying to threaten Ferris quietly while the parents are present
jokes.punchline: The attempted menace of 'close personal supervision' delivered in a fake-casual register is funny because Rooney has completely lost the room — he's now powerless and both he and Ferris know it
jokes.explanation: Rooney's shift from triumphant villain to impotent threatener is handled with good comic awareness. The 'close personal supervision' phrase is funny for trying to sound authoritative while having zero leverage.

jokes.text: Ferris's mom thanks Rooney for 'driving Ferris home from the hospital' — an entirely fictitious scenario Rooney has apparently been forced to play along with
jokes.setup: Rooney came to the Bueller house to catch Ferris; somehow the story has been flipped so he is now Ferris's benefactor
jokes.punchline: Mom's sincere gratitude for a rescue that never happened — with Rooney silently absorbing it — is a payoff to Ferris's endless ability to reshape reality to his advantage
