jokes.explanation: The inversion is elegant and deeply satisfying — Rooney, who has suffered the most, ends up thanked for helping. The audience understands the full humiliation even though the mom doesn't. Strong dramatic irony, well-earned.

jokes.text: 'Can you imagine someone as sick as Ferris trying to walk home from the hospital?' — delivered as the parents hustle Rooney out
jokes.setup: Ferris is visibly completely healthy; Mom is explaining to Rooney why Ferris was at the hospital
jokes.punchline: The rhetorical 'Can you imagine?' is delivered to the man who has spent all day trying to prove Ferris is faking — Rooney's silent reaction is the joke
jokes.explanation: The dramatic irony is rich — asking Rooney to sympathize with the fiction he's spent the day fighting to disprove. His reaction beat (forced to nod along) is likely the bigger laugh.

jokes.text: As Rooney is being thanked and ushered out like a hero, Jeanie calls after him: 'By the way, Mr. Rooney, you left your wallet on the kitchen floor.'
jokes.setup: Rooney was in the Bueller house trying to catch Ferris and has been thoroughly humiliated; he's now being graciously seen out
jokes.punchline: Jeanie's casual observation about the wallet is a final twist of the knife — confirming the full extent of Rooney's degradation, with the dropped wallet as evidence of his panic earlier
jokes.explanation: Perfectly economical delivery of maximum humiliation. Jeanie saying it in front of the parents — who have no idea why a principal would be dropping wallets on their kitchen floor — adds a layer. It also signals Jeanie's shift from adversary to quiet ally of Ferris.

jokes.text: Ferris, back in bed performing illness, announces he feels '150% better' and begs to go to school
jokes.setup: Parents are fussing over 'sick' Ferris in bed
jokes.punchline: Ferris claiming to feel '150% better' — a patently unbelievable number — while simultaneously begging to go to school (something no sick child ever does) is an absurd performance of wellness disguised as a performance of recovery
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the layers — Ferris is so good at manipulation that he even manages to seem reluctantly recovered, pleading to return to school to seem credible. The '150%' is a funny specific detail.

jokes.text: Mom asks 'How'd you get to be so sweet?' — Dad replies: 'Years of practice.'
jokes.setup: Dad has just told Ferris to stay in bed and rest — an act of parental kindness
jokes.punchline: His self-satisfied response 'Years of practice' to a compliment about his sweetness is a small, dry piece of self-deprecating vanity
jokes.explanation: A pleasant but unremarkable bit of dad-comedy. The line is harmless and gently funny but entirely generic — any sitcom dad could deliver it.

jokes.text: Ferris, alone in bed after successfully gaming the entire day, delivers his final monologue directly to camera: 'I said it before and I'll say it again. Life moves pretty fast. If you don't stop and look around once in a while, you could miss it.'
jokes.setup: Ferris has just pulled off an entire day of elaborate deception and adventure; the film is wrapping up
jokes.punchline: His delivery of this 'wisdom' — which is both genuinely sincere AND a bit of self-satisfied smugness from a character who gamed an entire city — lands as simultaneously earnest and lightly self-mocking
jokes.explanation: One of the most quoted lines in cinema. What makes it comedically exceptional — beyond its genuine philosophical resonance — is the meta-irony: Ferris has not 'stopped and looked around'; he has orchestrated an insanely complex, exhausting day of manipulation. Saying this from bed after successfully hoodwinking an entire city gives the line a smug undertone that makes it funnier on rewatch. The character integration is total — only Ferris can deliver this as both sincerely meant and completely self-serving. Earns the 8.5+ because it has become a cultural touchstone.

jokes.text: Rooney, now alone outside, delivers a defeated monologue: 'Four years of chasing this kid. Four years he has been making a fool of me.'
jokes.setup: Rooney has just been humiliated in every possible way — thanked for helping his nemesis, left with a lost wallet, seen out of the house like a guest
jokes.punchline: His quiet reckoning — four years of chasing, still losing — delivered with total defeat, is funny for its resigned accuracy
jokes.explanation: A satisfying character moment for Rooney. The comedy comes from the cumulative weight of the day settling on him. Not a sharp joke so much as a well-earned character beat.

jokes.text: A passing kid spots the battered, disheveled Rooney on the street and asks: 'Hey, Mr. Rooney, what's going on?' Then: 'Did you get in a fight?'
jokes.setup: Rooney has been beaten, bitten, humiliated, and dragged through a full day of indignities — he is visibly destroyed
jokes.punchline: A student's innocent inquiry confirms what the audience already knows: Rooney looks absolutely terrible. The 'Did you get in a fight?' is an understatement of Rooney's condition
jokes.explanation: A reliable visual comedy beat — the audience gets to see the full scope of Rooney's devastation reflected in a stranger's reaction. Well-placed but not exceptional.

jokes.text: The kid asks: 'Want a lift?' — Rooney, the principal who has spent all day failing to enforce rules, is reduced to accepting rides from students
jokes.setup: Rooney is stranded outside the Bueller house, destroyed, far from school
jokes.punchline: Being offered a lift by a student is the final indignity — an authority figure reduced to needing help from those he's supposed to supervise
jokes.explanation: The situational irony is effective — authority figure needing charity from his subjects. The humor is in the status inversion more than any specific line.

jokes.text: On the school bus, the kid tells Rooney: 'I bet you never smelled a real school bus before.'
jokes.setup: Rooney, a school administrator, is riding a student's school bus in defeat
jokes.punchline: The kid's observation implies Rooney has always been insulated from the actual experience of being a student — a final small humiliation that also carries ironic truth
jokes.explanation: A surprisingly sharp little line. 'A real school bus' implies Rooney has always experienced school as management, never as a student. It's also just a funny sensory specific — smelling a school bus. Good economy and a genuinely original angle on Rooney's humiliation.

jokes.text: The kid offers Rooney a Gummy Bear with the detail: 'They've been in my pocket. They're real warm and soft.'
jokes.setup: Rooney is riding in defeat on a school bus
jokes.punchline: The unsolicited detail 'They've been in my pocket — they're real warm and soft' transforms a simple offer into something deeply unpleasant. The specificity makes it funny — 'warm and soft' is exactly the wrong description for candy
jokes.explanation: One of the funnier jokes in the reel. The humor is entirely in the two adjectives — 'warm and soft.' No child would think these are off-putting descriptions, but every adult in the audience will recoil slightly. The specificity is the craft. It's a small absurdist cringe gem that earns its originality score.

jokes.text: Post-credits: Ferris appears on screen and says 'You're still here? It's over. Go home.' then 'Go.'
jokes.setup: The film has ended; a post-credits tag
jokes.punchline: Ferris breaks the fourth wall one final time to dismiss the audience — treating viewers who stayed for a secret ending as slightly pathetic for waiting
jokes.explanation: This is one of cinema's great post-credits gags and arguably the best joke in the reel. It works on multiple levels: (1) it's a perfect capstone to Ferris's fourth-wall relationship with the audience, (2) it's funny precisely because the people who stayed to watch it are being mocked for staying, (3) the economy is flawless — four words do everything. The originality was remarkable for 1986 and the character integration is total. Only Ferris Bueller could make this dismissal feel affectionate rather than mean. Earns the 9+ score.
